...the Arabic language has no (...) ever. This is the view of Mujahid, and it is the correct one: these letters have no meanings.

If someone says: How can you be certain that they have no meanings, when negation requires proof? We say: We are certain of this because the Qur'an was revealed in a clear Arabic tongue, and the Arabic language does not contain these alphabetic letters as meaningful words. In the language of the Arabs, these letters are simply letters from which speech is composed. However, some have said that these alphabetic letters have a purpose. What is the purpose? It is to demonstrate the inability of these deniers. This Qur'an is made of the same letters from which you compose your speech, and yet it has rendered you incapable. It has not brought anything new; it has only brought the letters from which you build your speech. He said: What supports this is that you hardly see a surah that begins with these letters without the mention of the Qur'an following it. He said: ﴿Alif, Lam, Meem. The revelation of the Book﴾ [As-Sajdah 1-2]. The Qur'an is meant by "the Book." It is called a "kitab" (book), and the word is on the pattern of fi'al in the sense of maf'ul (passive participle), meaning "written." It is called a book because it was written in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), in the scrolls in the hands of the angels, and in the scrolls in our hands. For this reason it is called a book.

He said: (mubtada'), which of them is the mubtada' (subject)? ﴿Tanzil (revelation)﴾, or ﴿al-Kitab (the Book)﴾? ﴿Tanzil﴾ is the subject, because "al-Kitab" is the genitive complement of it, so it is not the subject. (The subject is ﴿la rayba﴾, "there is no doubt," shakk ﴿fihi﴾, "in it," is the first predicate.)

﴿The revelation of the Book, there is no doubt in it﴾ [As-Sajdah 2]. This means that the revelation of the Book is affirmed, and there is no doubt in it. Is the negation here on its literal basis, or is it a negation meaning a prohibition, i.e., "do not doubt it"?

There are two opinions. Some scholars say that the negation here carries the sense of a prohibition, so the meaning of "there is no doubt in it" is: do not doubt it.

Others among the people of knowledge say that the negation is meant in its literal sense: this Book contains no doubt. And if there is no doubt in it, it follows that doubting it is forbidden, because if doubt has been negated from the Qur'an, it is not lawful for us to doubt it. This view is more emphatic in its negation: there is no doubt in it, whether or not anyone doubts it. So it is literally "there is no doubt in it."

As for the word "rayb," the author says it means doubt (shakk). However, some scholars held that no two words are exact synonyms, and that there must be a difference between them. They said: "rayb" is doubt accompanied by anxiety and disquiet (ribah). It is not merely doubt in general; it is a specific kind of doubt, in which there is anxiety and suspicion, and the soul is preoccupied with it, unlike doubt that carries no such disquiet.

His statement: (﴿from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [As-Sajdah 2] is the second predicate). The meaning is: the revelation of the Book is affirmed, there is no doubt in it, [it is] the revelation of the Book from the Lord of the worlds. On this basis, is the first predicate a clause or not? The first predicate, "there is no doubt in it," is a clause, because ﴿la﴾ is the negation of the genus, ﴿rayba﴾ is its noun, and ﴿fihi﴾ is its predicate, so it is a clause. The second predicate, "from the Lord of the worlds," is a prepositional phrase, because it is a preposition with its object.

His statement: ﴿from the Lord of the worlds﴾. ﴿Rabb al-'alamin (the Lord of the worlds)﴾ is the One who created them, owns them, and owns the authority to dispose of them. Lordship (rububiyyah) includes three things: creation, ownership, and management.

His statement: ﴿al-'alamin (the worlds)﴾. It refers to everything other than Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Everything other than Allah is called "'alam" (world) because each of them is a sign (ʿalam) pointing to its Creator. There is nothing except that it contains a sign from the signs of Allah, the Glorified and Exalted, testifying to His oneness, power, might, and other attributes.

His statement: ﴿The revelation of the Book, there is no doubt in it, from the Lord of the worlds﴾. This means that this revelation of the Book is from Allah, and there is no ambiguity about it. It is not the word of Muhammad, nor the word of Jibril, nor the word of any creature. Rather, it is from the Lord of the worlds alone. In terms of i'rab (grammatical analysis), it is permissible to make ﴿la rayba fihi﴾ a circumstantial phrase (hal) in the accusative position: this Book, free from doubt, from where is it? ﴿From the Lord of the worlds﴾. It is also permissible to make ﴿la rayba fihi﴾ a single predicate, with ﴿from the Lord of the worlds﴾ as a circumstantial phrase of ﴿la rayba fihi﴾. (...) that you make the two clauses both predicates, or one of them a predicate and the other a circumstantial phrase.

In any case, the meaning of the noble verse is that the revelation of the Book is a matter about which there is no doubt, and that it is also from the Lord of the worlds, about which there is no doubt.

In my view, the best thing to say about the i'rab is that we make ﴿the revelation of the Book from the Lord of the worlds﴾, and ﴿la rayba fihi﴾ is the circumstantial phrase. The revelation of the Book is from the Lord of the worlds, not from anyone else, and ﴿la rayba fihi﴾ is a circumstantial phrase.

Then he said: (﴿am (or)﴾, meaning ﴿bal (rather)﴾, ﴿they say, he has invented it﴾ [As-Sajdah 3], meaning Muhammad). The author says that ﴿am﴾ carries the sense of ﴿bal﴾. So it is a transitional retraction (idrab intiqali), not a nullifying retraction (idrab ibtali), because it does not nullify what preceded it. Yet it still carries the meaning of ﴿bal﴾ and the interrogative hamzah. In origin, they would say: "Rather, do they say he has invented it?" The interrogation in this verse is for denial, as shown by his statement "no," meaning that it is not invented.

The meaning of "iftira'" (invention)... what is the meaning of iftira'? It is lying. So the meaning of ﴿iftarahu (he has invented it)﴾ is: he lied by claiming that it is from Allah.

Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Rather, it is the truth﴾ [As-Sajdah 3]. ﴿Bal (rather)﴾ here is ... ? It is a nullifying retraction (idrab ibtali).

He said: Rather, it, meaning the Qur'an or the Book as Allah expressed it: ﴿Rather, it is the truth from your Lord﴾. Rather, it is the truth, meaning the established one that does not waver, and it is the truth that encompasses every good.

His statement: ﴿from your Lord﴾ is a prepositional phrase functioning as a circumstantial phrase of ﴿huwa (it)﴾, meaning: while it is from your Lord. Reflect on the first verse, where He said: ﴿from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [As-Sajdah 2], and here He said: ﴿from your Lord﴾. Why? Because who was accused of inventing it? The Messenger (ﷺ). So Allah wanted to show that the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) could not invent lies, because he has a special lordship, which is His saying: ﴿from your Lord﴾. So the lordship here is a special lordship. Then Allah explained the wisdom behind this in His saying: ﴿that you may warn a people﴾ and so on [As-Sajdah 3].

(...) from the Lord of the worlds, and here He said: from your Lord (...). What is the wisdom in the difference of expression between His saying ﴿from the Lord of the worlds﴾ and His saying ﴿from your Lord﴾?

The wisdom is that when He wanted to inform about the Qur'an as the Qur'an, He showed that it was sent down from the Lord of the worlds, on whom these (...) rely, and so the Book is sent down to him. Since He is the Lord of the worlds, all the worlds must accept this, because it is from their Lord.

As for the second, ﴿from your Lord﴾, since the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) was attributed with lying about this Qur'an, Allah mentioned His special lordship: ﴿from your Lord﴾, indicating that he is the Messenger of Allah, because the one who sent down the Qur'an is his Lord, who (...) nurtures him with a special lordship. Do you understand now? In the first, from the perspective of describing the Qur'an as a Qur'an, He said: a revelation from the Lord of the worlds. In the second (...): ﴿Rather, it is the truth from your Lord﴾ [As-Sajdah 3], who nurtures you with a special lordship, so you are His Messenger.

Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿that you may warn a people﴾ [As-Sajdah 3]. ﴿Li-tundhira (that you may warn)﴾, (...) is omitted, and its estimate is (...). However, there is some discussion on the matter (...) an object, so there is a discussion. But there is no doubt that the estimate is "bihi (with it)," because it is the instrument of warning by which one warns, i.e., because of it. However, the second object is omitted, with a different estimate from the one the author mentioned: "that you may warn them with it, a people, of the punishment." I chose this because of His saying: ﴿Say, I have warned you of a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt of 'Ad﴾ [Fussilat 13]. Allah clarified in another verse what is warned of.

(﴿that you may warn a people﴾, ma is a negation particle) ﴿no warner had come to them before you, that they might be guided﴾.

﴿that you may warn a people to whom no warner had come﴾. The author says that ﴿ma﴾ is a negation particle. His saying in Surah Ya-Sin: ﴿that you may warn a people whose fathers had not been warned, so they are unaware﴾ [Ya-Sin 6]. What the author established, that ﴿ma﴾ is a negation particle, is the correct view regarding its i'rab, although some have said it is a relative pronoun, meaning: that you may warn a people, the warnings that came to them before you, i.e., warn them of the punishment. According to this view, ﴿ma﴾ is a relative pronoun and is the second object of ﴿tundhira (you warn)﴾. But the view the author followed is more correct, that ﴿ma﴾ is a negation particle.

So the summary of the i'rab of ﴿ma﴾ is two opinions:
One: that it is a negation particle, so the meaning of the noble verse is: that you may warn a people to whom no warner came before you.
The second view: that ﴿ma﴾ is a relative pronoun, meaning: that you may warn a people, the warnings that came to them before you.
The correct one is the first.

No messenger was sent to the Arabs after Isma'il except Muhammad (ﷺ). For this reason the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "I am the answer to the prayer of my father Abraham" [Narrated by Ahmad (17150), and al-Hakim, whose wording it is (3566), from the hadith of al-'Irbad ibn Sariyah, may Allah be pleased with him], referring to His saying: ﴿Our Lord, send among them a messenger from themselves who will recite to them Your verses﴾ [Al-Baqarah 129], to the end.

His saying: ﴿no warner had come to them before you﴾. If someone asks: What is the benefit of describing these people as having had no warner come to them before?

The benefit of this is two things:
The first: to show the great need they had for the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him), since they were in the utmost need of his being sent.
The second: to show Allah's favor upon them through this Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him), since he is the Messenger who came to them, and no warner came before him.

His saying: ﴿that you may warn a people to whom no warner had come before you, that they might be guided﴾. Such an expression occurs often in the Noble Qur'an: ﴿that they might be guided﴾, ﴿that you may be grateful﴾, ﴿that you may be successful﴾. Is it for hope (raja') or for expectation (tawaqqu')?

Some said: It is for hope, but in terms of the state of the addressee, not the state of the speaker. Why not in terms of the state of the speaker? Because Allah, the Exalted... (...) His creation, since hope is the longing to attain what is difficult to reach. It may not be impossible, but it is hoped for, and there is some (...) in it. The Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, cannot be described this way. So it is hope in terms of the state of the addressee.

We said: ﴿la'alla (that/perhaps)﴾ indicates causation. Is it a deficiency for Allah to make one thing the cause of another? No. It is part of His perfection, glorified and exalted, that He connects things with their causes. This view is refuted: the cause is inseparable from its effect. So if He says here ﴿that they might be guided﴾, it follows that they should be guided, since this has a cause, and the cause is inseparable from its effect. Because this warner has claimed that he must be followed.

The answer to this is to say: the cause is of two kinds: the moving cause (ʿillah ba'ithah) and the final cause (ʿillah ghaʾiyyah). The moving cause may be necessitating or non-necessitating. This is like His saying: ﴿I did not create the jinn and mankind except that they should worship Me﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat 56], although not all of them worship Him. And like His saying: ﴿And We did not send any messenger except to be obeyed by permission of Allah﴾ [An-Nisa' 64]. It is well known that many messengers were disobeyed and not obeyed. Here the moving cause is non-necessitating; that is, the wisdom behind it is this, and it may or may not be realized. They illustrated this with the saying: "I sharpened the pen so that I may write with it," or for this purpose. But must you write or not? You may write, or you may not write.

﴿that they might be guided﴾. Guidance here includes the guidance of direction (hidayat al-dalalah) and the guidance of success (hidayat al-tawfiq). The Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) brought the guidance of direction, while success is in the hand of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and there is no success except after knowledge.

(﴿that they might be guided﴾ by your warning).

Then He said: ﴿Allah is the One who created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days﴾ [As-Sajdah 4]. ﴿Allah﴾ is the subject, ﴿alladhi (the One who)﴾ is a relative pronoun functioning as the predicate, and ﴿khalaqa (created)﴾ means "brought into existence with measure and order." Originally, in the language, khalq means measuring, as in the words of the poet:

"Indeed you measure what you create, while some people create but do not measure."

Khalq is also applied to bringing into existence with measure, which is what is meant here. As for His saying ﴿al-samawat (the heavens)﴾, they are the visible bodies, and they are seven. And ﴿al-ard (the earth)﴾ is meant as a genus, encompassing all the earths.

﴿He created the heavens and the earth and what is between them﴾. That is, what is between them. What is between them? Is it the clouds or not? Likewise the stars, the moon, the sun, and similar things. This shows that there are things we do not yet know. Until now, science discovers many things between the sky and the earth. It also shows that what is between the heavens and the earth is not merely the clouds. Rather, Allah has made it a counterpart to the creation of the heavens and the earth, so it must be something great that corresponds to these creations.

﴿and what is between them in six days﴾. He said: (The first of them is Sunday and the last is Friday). Allah has explained these six days in Surah Fussilat, when He said: ﴿Say, do you indeed disbelieve in He who created the earth in two days and attribute to Him equals? That is the Lord of the worlds. And He placed firmly on it [mountains] from above it and blessed it and determined therein its sustenance in four days, complete for those who ask﴾ [Fussilat 9-10]. Do you understand now? How many days did He create the earth? In four days. ﴿And He placed in it firm mountains﴾, up to His saying: ﴿in four days﴾. ﴿Then He turned to the heaven while it was smoke and said to it and to the earth: come willingly or by compulsion. They said: We come willingly. Then He completed them as seven heavens in two days﴾ [Fussilat 11-12]. So the days are six, the first being Sunday and the last Friday. Were these days like our days, or was each day the length of a thousand years, or were they days in the sense of hours or moments? There are opinions. Some said they are days, meaning moments, because when Allah wills something He says to it "Be," and it is. The term "days" is used to express time in general.

Others said they are days, each day being the length of a thousand years, so how many years would that make? Six thousand years.

Others said they are days like our days, because when the word "days" is used without qualification, it refers to these known days. Especially since in Surah Fussilat it was specified as ﴿in four days﴾ and ﴿in two days﴾. So we cannot, by the indication of the Qur'an, depart from what is known and familiar in the Arabic language.

If someone says: Although this view is apparent from the Qur'an, two issues are raised against it. The first issue is that when the heavens and the earth were created, there was no sun by which days could be measured, so what do we say?

* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: The main point is the measure of these days. The second issue (...) is to ask: why was it not in a moment, or why was it not in very long days, in a moment (...) the power of Allah, "Be, and it is," whatever (...) testing these creatures. That is, a thousand years is not enough, nor two thousand, nor a hundred thousand, for they are numerous creatures that are not enough (...). So either they are measured by the power of Allah, or they are measured according to their reality. If you measure them by the power of Allah, the six days have no meaning; it is in a moment. If you measure them according to their reality, setting aside the power of Allah (...), there were millions of years in it, because the creatures are very great and arranged in the utmost order.

The answer to this is to take these two objections: the first, we have already understood the answer to it, and the year is according to the knowledge of Allah, and Allah knows (...).

As for the second, the answer to it is to say: this is what Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said, and it is not for us to exceed what Allah has told us, because this is a matter we cannot encompass. Allah, the Exalted, has said: ﴿I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth, nor the creation of themselves﴾ [Al-Kahf 51].

We say about these matters: according to the power of Allah, not according to our reality (...) Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. So it must be measured by the power of Allah, and it is said: their being six days is according to what the power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, requires. And it is not for us to (...).

Therefore the Jews, may Allah's curse be upon them, said: Allah the Exalted created the heavens and the earth in six days, then on the Sabbath He rested, — we seek refuge in Allah — because the day of God's rest is their festival, so they made their festival the Sabbath. They lied in this; Allah the Mighty and Majestic does not tire, so as to need rest.

He says: ﴿Then He rose over the Throne﴾. "Istawa" means "ʿalā" (rose above, ascended). Istawa a thing... We have mentioned previously that istawa occurs in the Qur'an in three forms: absolute, restricted with "ilā" (to), and restricted with "ʿalā" (upon) (...) in four forms: absolute, with "ilā", restricted with "ʿalā", and restricted with the particle of accompaniment (wāw al-maʿīyah). When it comes absolute, it means "became complete," as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when he reached his maturity and was fully developed﴾ [al-Qasas 14] (...). When restricted with "ilā," it means intention (...) as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then He turned to the heaven while it was smoke﴾ [Fussilat 11]. In this verse there is a second view, that ﴿istawā﴾ means "rose above," then He ascended to it, so that this is like the other attributes which (...).

The third form: restricted with "ʿalā," which carries the meaning of elevation and settling, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So when you and those with you are settled upon the ship﴾ [al-Muʾminun 28], and as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿That you may sit firmly upon its backs﴾ [az-Zukhruf 13], meaning: that you may rise above their backs and settle. It never comes in the Arabic language with any other meaning; when it is followed by "ʿalā," it comes only with this meaning (...); it never has any other meaning.

The fourth: restricted with the particle of accompaniment, so it means "equalled" — "istawā" meaning "equalled," as in the saying of the Arabs: "istawā al-māʾ wa al-khashabah," meaning the water became equal to the wood (...) He rose over the Throne.

It never comes in the language with any other meaning at all. It has come in the Noble Qur'an in seven places, in none of which is there a single instance where the expression differs from this: ﴿Then He rose over the Throne﴾ [al-Aʿraf 54], ﴿The Most Merciful rose over the Throne﴾ [Taha 5], and what resembles them. According to the people of the Sunnah and the Jama'ah, it means: He rose over the Throne and settled upon it. It is also reported from them: "He rose (irtafaʿa)," and reported from them: "He ascended (ṣaʿida)." Irtafaʿa, ṣaʿida, and ʿalā have close meanings; therefore we have chosen to say: "in the sense of rising above and settling." As for "irtafaʿa" and "ṣaʿida" (...).

This meaning of istawā, the meaning of elevation and settling, may encounter a question, and it is said: Do you not say that Allah the Mighty and Majestic's elevation by His Essence is an essential, eternal, everlasting attribute? What do we say?

We say: Yes, we say that Allah the Mighty and Majestic's elevation by His Essence is an eternal, everlasting attribute which does not cease to be with Allah (...) He created, then rose over; the meaning of that is that (...) He is not risen over the Throne.

We say: Yes, this is true; because rising over the Throne is more specific than absolute elevation. Elevation is necessary; rising over the Throne, elevation specifically upon the Throne, is a specific meaning distinct from the meaning of absolute elevation. Is it clear or not?

So He, Glorified and Exalted, is always elevated, but His being upon the Throne itself is something that occurred, certainly occurred, because the Throne is created, and Allah has made clear that He rose over the Throne after creating the heavens and the earth. Yes, and whether (...) before that, Allah knows best; we do not know.

But the question now: if you say that the meaning of "rose over the Throne" is "rose above it and settled upon it," an objection arises for us. What is the objection? What is (...) We say that the elevation of Allah the Mighty and Majestic is an essential, eternal, everlasting attribute, so how do you say that the meaning of "rose over the Throne" is "rose above it," while you say that elevation is an essential, eternal, everlasting attribute?

We say: Elevation is of two kinds: absolute elevation, and elevation specific to the Throne.

The first, which is absolute elevation, is an essential, eternal, everlasting attribute: that Allah has not ceased and does not cease being elevated by His Essence above all creation.

As for rising over the Throne, it is a voluntary (fiʿliyyah) attribute specific to whom? To the Throne.

Let me give an example that brings the meaning closer: when a person is on the roof, he is elevated above what is beneath the roof, isn't he? Then if a chair is placed on the roof and he sits on it, his elevation upon this chair becomes a specific elevation, alongside the continuing first elevation, which is absolute elevation; but this is a specific elevation upon this chair.

Thus it is clear that there is a difference between elevation in the general sense, which is an essential, eternal, everlasting attribute, and rising over the Throne, which is a specific elevation over that Throne. For this reason, some of the early generation (salaf) are reported to have explained it as "He sat upon it," and this is close to explaining it as "settling." So this is a specific elevation; there is a difference between specific elevation and elevation in the general sense. Is it clear, O brothers?

We move from this meaning to the question: is rising over the Throne one of the voluntary attributes or one of the essential attributes?

The answer: it is one of the voluntary attributes, because everything that is connected to the will (...) is one of the voluntary attributes; therefore rising over the Throne is one of the voluntary attributes.

The people of the Sunnah and the Jama'ah say: He rose over the Throne, meaning He rose above it and settled. And how was that elevation and settling?

We do not know; it is obligatory to pause. For this reason, Imam Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, when he was asked — it was said to him: "O Abu ʿAbd Allah, ﴿The Most Merciful rose over the Throne﴾ [Taha 5], how did He rise?" He lowered his head — may Allah have mercy on him — until sweat covered him, from the intensity of the impact of this question on his heart. Then he raised his head and said: "The istiwa' is not unknown, the how (kayf) is not conceivable, belief in it is obligatory, and asking about it is an innovation." It is related from Malik in another form that he said: "The istiwa' is known, the how is unknown, belief in it is obligatory, and asking about it is an innovation."

But what is authentically transmitted from him with a chain is the first wording: "The istiwa' is not unknown, the how is not conceivable, belief in it is obligatory, and asking about it is an innovation." Then he said: "I do not see you except as an innovator."

Although it is possible that he was a questioner seeking clarification, not a questioner testing him; therefore he said: "I do not see you, or I do not think you, except as an innovator," then he ordered him to be removed (...).

The summary is that we say: istiwa' is not unknown, or it is known in meaning in the Arabic language, and the Qur'an was revealed in the Arabic language, so what is its meaning linguistically? "ʿalā" (rose) and "irtafaʿa" (ascended).

("The how is not conceivable") means: we do not conceive it. This is more emphatic than the word "unknown," meaning the intellect cannot grasp or encompass it, because Allah is greater than that the intellects could grasp the essence of His Self and His attributes. Then, when the rational proof is absent, what remains? The transmitted proof, and the transmission has not come with mention of the modality.

So when both the rational proof and the transmitted proof are absent, it is obligatory to pause. For this reason the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, adopted the side of pausing, even though they were more eager than us for good and for knowledge. Did they ask the Messenger ﷺ, saying: "How did He rise?" or not? No. For this reason he said: "asking about it is an innovation": asking about it, meaning about the modality, is an innovation; the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, did not ask about this, and it cannot be reached. So asking about it is an overreach in that it cannot be attained, and an innovation in that the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, did not ask about it.

("Belief in it is obligatory") — belief in what? In the istiwa' over the Throne is obligatory. Why? Why is it obligatory? Because Allah informed of it about Himself, and what Allah informs about Himself we are obliged to accept, and not to measure it by our intellects. So, praise be to Allah, the istiwa' is now clear: the meaning of istiwa' is elevation and settling, and its meaning is known; but the modality is unknown and inconceivable, meaning the intellect does not grasp it, nor (...) upon it, and the transmitted text has not indicated it, so it is obligatory to pause. But is there a modality to His istiwa'? It is unknown; for this reason he said: "The how is unknown, belief in it is obligatory, and asking about it is an innovation."

(...) It is impossible that He rose over the Throne, meaning rose above it and settled; rather its meaning is that He took control of the Throne, prevailed, and possessed. And that istiwa' includes this meaning — or have you found this in the dictionaries of the language? They said: We found it in the saying of the poet:

"Bishr has taken control of Iraq, without sword or spilled blood."

"Istawā ʿalā al-ʿIrāq" means: he took control of it. So they return Allah's speech to this verse, recited in the time of Bishr ibn Marwan when he took control of Iraq. This verse is said to have an unknown composer, not known. Glory be to Allah, that the Noble Qur'an should be based on a line of poetry whose composer is unknown; and I think we all know that when a report contains an unknown narrator, it is rejected (...). Then we say: Supposing the composer is known and that he is among the pure Arabs whose tongues were not contaminated by foreign speech, still, "istawā ʿalā al-ʿIrāq" cannot properly be understood as "rose above Iraq" in a non-physical, moral elevation; rather the sense of physical elevation should be that Iraq is something a man cannot sit upon, isn't that so? Then the obstacle here is a rational matter, and the istiwa' here would be a moral istiwa', meaning he rose over it with a moral elevation. And if we interpret it as "rose over it with moral elevation," it becomes more emphatic than interpreting it as "took control," more emphatic; because mere taking control may not involve elevation; one may be in control yet be like nothing. So when we say "istawā" means "rose with moral elevation," it becomes more emphatic in possession and subjugation. Is it clear? So it is clear that there is no proof in this verse under any circumstance.

Moreover, it contradicts the apparent meaning of the Qur'an and contradicts what the early generation and the imams agreed upon, that istiwa' means elevation and settling; so this is false.

Therefore what we believe is that Allah the Exalted rose over His Throne in a manner befitting His majesty, meaning He rose above it and settled. The author says: it is in language "the king's throne." So istiwa' over the Throne is a special throne, isn't it? A special throne befitting (...); Allah the Exalted said about the Queen of Sheba, when the hoopoe informed about her: ﴿And she has a mighty throne﴾ [an-Naml 23], and He said in the story of Yusuf: ﴿And he raised his parents upon the throne, and they fell down before him in prostration﴾ [Yusuf 100], meaning: the throne specific to the king, so it must be a throne magnified according to his kingship. This is the throne. Therefore the Throne of the Most Merciful, Mighty and Majestic, is the greatest thing, because it is the throne of the greatest of beings, who is Allah the Mighty and Majestic. For this reason it is reported in a hadith that the seven heavens and the seven earths, compared to the Kursi, are like a ring cast into a desert of the earth — a ring (...), small, cast into a desert of the earth. If a ring were cast into a desert of the earth, could it be compared to the desert? How great is the ratio? Not one of (...). "And the excellence of the Throne over the Kursi is like the excellence of the desert over this ring." So the Kursi compared to the Throne is like a ring cast into a desert of the earth; and through this you know the magnitude of the greatness of the Creator, Glorified and Exalted, who created these great things.

The author says: "istiwa' befitting Him." We want to discuss with the author this phrase: does this statement indicate that he follows the early generation's (salaf) interpretation of istiwa', or the later scholars' (khalaf) position?

* Student: We do not know.

* The Shaykh: We do not know; because the istiwa' that befits Him, according to the later scholars, they say: the istiwa' that befits Him is istilaʾ (domination), this is what they say among them. The early generation say: the istiwa' that befits Him is elevation in the manner that befits Allah, and this is expressed by many people (...) the word istiwa' (...).

This statement is general, so you must add to it: istawā, meaning rose above and settled, istiwa' befitting Him.

He said: ﴿You have not, besides Him, any protector or intercessor﴾ [as-Sajdah 4]. ﴿You have﴾: "mā" is negating, and the address in His saying ﴿lakum﴾ — the author said: "O disbelievers of Makkah." The correct view is generality, meaning: "what you (plural) have," addressed to all, including the disbelievers of Makkah and others.

﴿From besides Him, any protector﴾: "dūn" means "other than," meaning: what you have other than Him. Therefore the author said: "from other than Him, ﴿any protector﴾: the subject of (mā) with the addition of (min)." Where is the subject of (mā)?

﴿Mā lakum﴾ — this is "mā"; and he says: ﴿min walī﴾, the subject of (mā) with the addition of (min), and its addition here is for emphasis and explicit generality. But his saying "the subject of (mā)" — is there an i'rab issue in it?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: The subject of (mā) is negating.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: The i'rab of his saying "the subject of (mā)" only. What does Ibn Malik say?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No.

"...........  with the continuance of negation and the ordering, it is attached"

So it is necessary for (mā) that it be in order, meaning the noun before the predicate. If it is not so, it does not operate; for (mā) only operates in the dialect of the Hijazis under the conditions Ibn Malik mentioned. So the author's statement "the subject of (mā)" is a slip of the pen or an oversight, for here (mā) is not operative; here (mā) is merely negating, and the reason its operation is void is the absence of ordering.

Where is the predicate of the subject? The predicate of the subject, which is what is "mā"'s predicate? The predicate of the subject is the phrase ﴿lakum﴾: ﴿Mā lakum min dūnihi min walī﴾. He says: "(i.e., a helper) ﴿nor an intercessor﴾." He explained "walī" here as "helper," and they objected to this, because Allah says in another verse: ﴿You have not, besides Allah, any protector or helper﴾ [al-Baqarah 107], and conjunction requires difference, that the helper is other than the protector. Therefore it is better to explain "walī" as one who takes charge of a person's affairs, taking charge of his affairs by bringing good to him and warding off harm from him. Then if it is joined with "naṣīr" (helper), it becomes specific to bringing good, and the helper to repelling evil. So the meaning of ﴿min walī﴾ is: from one who takes charge of his affairs by bringing good to him and warding off evil from him.

And His saying ﴿nor an intercessor﴾ means: an intercessor who intercedes for you. Therefore he said: "﴿Nor an intercessor﴾ who repels His punishment from you." This too needs review, for the intercessor does not repel; rather he intercedes and asks. The repeller is the helper and the protector; as for the intercessor, he does not repel, but mediates. For this reason they defined intercession as: mediation for another in order to bring benefit or repel harm — mediation for another, because the intercessor comes as an intercessor for the one interceded for, having been one and becoming two. So the correct view is that what is meant by the intercessor is: an intercessor who intercedes for you with Allah.

So we now have no one who takes charge of us other than Allah, and no one who intercedes for us with Allah the Mighty and Majestic. Thus ﴿You have not, besides Him, any protector or intercessor﴾; therefore intercession is only by Allah's permission, isn't it? ﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾ [al-Baqarah 255].

He said: "(﴿Will you not then remember?﴾ [as-Sajdah 4] — this, so that you believe?)" ﴿Will you not then remember?﴾ — it has passed us repeatedly that grammarians see two possibilities in parsing such a sentence:

The first possibility: the interrogative hamza enters upon something omitted that fits the context, and the fa' is conjunctive upon that omitted thing.

The second possibility: the hamza enters upon the sentence that follows the conjunction, and the conjunction is conjunctive upon what preceded.

We said that this second possibility is easier, because the first requires supposition, and the supposed item may be difficult, since it may be unclear to a person how it fits the context. So if you say: the hamza is for interrogation and is placed before the conjunction, and fa' is a conjunction, and the thing conjoined to is what preceded, and the construction without advancing or delaying is "fa-a-lā tatadhakkarūn."

The author said: "(this, so that you believe)." The author, may Allah have mercy on him, informed us by saying "this" that the intended meaning of "remember" is to perceive it and know it. It may also be that the intended meaning of "remember" is to be admonished, and on this basis it is intransitive, not transitive; meaning: will you not be admonished after you have known His great creatures, His istiwa' over His Throne, and that you have no protector or intercessor besides Him? Will you not be admonished so that you believe?

﴿He manages the affair from the heaven to the earth﴾: during the duration of the world; ﴿then it ascends to Him in a day the measure of which is a thousand years of what you count﴾ [as-Sajdah 5]: in the world. And in Surah al-Maʿārij: ﴿fifty thousand years﴾ [al-Maʿārij 4], and that is the Day of Resurrection because of its terrors relative to the disbeliever.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 32, verse 1 (part 3 of 4):

﴿He manages the affair from the heaven to the earth.﴾ His saying: ﴿from the heaven to the earth﴾. What is meant by "the heaven" here is those known and familiar celestial bodies. He manages it from the heaven to the earth, then it ascends to Him. "Ascends" means returns to Him. How does it descend from the heaven to the earth and then ascend to Him? What is it that ascends to Him? Is it the affair itself, or what results from that affair? What results from that affair. As for the affair, it descends. For example, if Allah, glorified and exalted, commands that this man worship Allah, the worship happens, and then the reward or punishment for the deed returns to Him according to what this servant does. Likewise, the affair descends from the heaven with the descent of rain, and then the effect of this thing returns to Him, in that it descended and gave life to the earth after its death, and similar things.

So the affair descends, and what else? It rises from the heaven to the earth, then it ascends to Him, that is, to Allah. "Ascends" means rises. But the author, may Allah have mercy on him, explained the verse as meaning that He manages it from the heaven to the earth in this world, then it returns to Him in the Hereafter, and then it ascends to Him in the Hereafter. He made the ascent mean the return, and there is no doubt that this is distortion (tahrif), because ascent is not the same as return, is it? Yes. What is the meaning of ascent?
* A student: Rising.
* The Shaykh: Rising. It rises to Him. The meaning is not that it returns to Him on the Day of Resurrection so that He rewards or punishes for it. The author made ﴿He manages the affair from the heaven﴾ refer to this world, in every (...) this world, the management of an affair that descends from the heaven to the earth. As for the ascent, it occurs on the Day of Resurrection, and he explained it as return.

According to the author's view, ﴿in a day whose measure is a thousand years of what you count﴾ contradicts what Allah mentioned in Surah al-Ma'arij (Sa'ala), because in Surah al-Ma'arij He said: ﴿fifty thousand years﴾ [al-Ma'arij 4]. The author answered in a way that implies the measure differs according to people. It will be for some people as fifty thousand years, for others as a thousand years, and for others as the time needed to perform an obligatory prayer. As he said: as for the believer, it will be lighter for him than an obligatory prayer he performed in this world, as came in the hadith:[[Ahmad recorded (11717) with his chain from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: It was said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "A day whose measure is fifty thousand years, how long this day is!" The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "By Him in whose hand my soul is, it will be made light for the believer, until it is lighter for him than an obligatory prayer that he performed in the world."]]

So the summary of the author's view is that the management of the affair from the heaven to the earth is when? In this world, from its beginning to its end. And that the ascent to Allah with this affair is when? In the Hereafter. He explained the ascent as return, fleeing from affirming intrinsic elevation (al-'uluww al-dhati).

The author faces a problem: if we make the return occur on the Day of Resurrection, then here in the verse it is a thousand years, and in Surah al-Ma'arij it is fifty thousand years.

The author's answer is that it is said: the difference in measure here is considered in terms of people's conditions. Some are made light for, until it is like a thousand years, and indeed it may be like the performance of an obligatory prayer. And some are made heavy, until it is the measure of fifty thousand years. Do you understand?

As for the correct view, which Ibn Kathir and most of the exegetes follow, they say: all of this, the management and the ascent, is in this world. Allah, glorified and exalted, manages the affair from the heaven to the earth, then it ascends to Him. Do the effects of this management ascend in this world or in the Hereafter? In this world. The meaning of ﴿in a day whose measure is a thousand years﴾ is that the distance between the heaven and the earth is five hundred years. This descent and its distance, and the ascent over the same distance, are five hundred years, so the whole is a thousand. So the meaning of His saying ﴿in a day whose measure is a thousand years﴾ is in terms of the descent and in terms of the ascent.

And His saying: ﴿in a day whose measure﴾. ﴿in a day﴾: must it be a complete day, or does ﴿in﴾ indicate a container (zarfiyyah) and not require totality (istiy'ab)?

The answer: ﴿in﴾ indicates a container and does not necessitate totality. That is, it is not necessary that the affair descends, for example, at the dawn prayer and ascends only at sunset. It is not necessary. It may descend and ascend in a moment, according to what Allah, mighty and majestic, wills, because ﴿in﴾ does not require totality. If you say: "I visited you on Sunday," does that require that the visit covered the entire day? No, but at a time within this day.

So ﴿in a day﴾ means at a time within this day, and this day was of a measure of a thousand years.
* A student: Regarding (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, so it came in the hadith: in every heaven is five hundred years, and between every heaven and (...) is five hundred years.
* A student: It mentioned a thousand years (...), although the distance to Allah, mighty and majestic, is many times greater.
* The Shaykh: No, He said: ﴿from the heaven to the earth﴾, meaning the lowest heaven to the earth.
* A student: To Allah.
* The Shaykh: No, it is not to Allah, it is from the heaven.
* A student: ﴿to Him﴾, to the heaven?
* The Shaykh: To the heaven, yes. ﴿from the heaven to the earth﴾, then it ascends to Him or to Allah, the Exalted. It is not necessary that Allah be in the lowest heaven.
* A student: (...) this verse ﴿a thousand years of what you count﴾ after people enter Paradise and Hell, and the verse of Sa'ala means (...).
* The Shaykh: When people enter Paradise and Hell, there is no end to it, forever and ever.

* * *

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿That is the Knower of the unseen﴾ [al-Sajdah 6]. (﴿That﴾ refers to the Creator who manages.) He used the demonstrative that indicates distance, because of the greatness of His station and His exaltedness, blessed and exalted is He.

His saying: "the Creator who manages." Which of these two attributes were mentioned previously? Only these two? Yes. The Creator who is established on His throne, who manages His creation. Istiwa' on the Throne is among the most important matters in this context, because despite His exaltedness, nothing hidden or witnessed is concealed from Him. So the author should have mentioned it along with this. He is the Creator, He is the Manager, and He is established on His throne. Despite His exaltedness and His establishment on His throne, nothing is hidden from Him. And with His creation and His management, is anything hidden from Him or not? Nothing is hidden from Him. For this reason, the Lord, mighty and majestic, knows you better than you know yourself, because He is the Creator. He created your body and He makes it grow. When the body grows by the weight of an atom, Allah the Exalted has created this growth. Do you perceive what grows in your body by the weight of an atom? No. So Allah knows you better than you know yourself, because He is the Creator, He is the Manager, and He is established on His throne.

(﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾: that is, what is absent from creation and what is present.) The unseen is what is absent from creation, and it is of two kinds: absolute unseen, which no one knows except Allah, and relative unseen, which is absent from one person but not absent from another.

Which of these two is meant? Both. He, glorified and exalted, knows what is absent from creation as absolutely unseen, so that no one knows it, and what is absent from them as relatively unseen. For example, now the person in the street is absent from us and we do not know him, but those there know him, and what is here we know, and they do not know it. This unseen is what?
* A student: Relative.
* The Shaykh: Relative. As for the knowledge of the future and what will happen of what Allah has not informed us of, it is absolute unseen.

﴿the witnessed﴾: he says it means presence, because shahida means to be present, and it also means to inform. It has several meanings. Here the meaning of "witnessed" is the present. So He knows the unseen and the present, glorified and exalted.

(﴿The Mighty﴾: the invulnerable in His dominion. ﴿The Merciful﴾: toward the people of His obedience.) ﴿The Mighty﴾: the author explained it as invulnerable in His dominion, and he often recurs in the author's tafsir saying: the Mighty means the Overpowering. We have previously stated that the Mighty is the one characterized by might, and that might has three meanings: might of standing (qadr), might of subjugation (qahr), and might of inaccessibility (imtina').

When you say: "This thing is 'aziz," meaning it has standing, as one says to his brother: "You are 'aziz to me," meaning you have standing and status with me.

And the might of subjugation, as it is said: ﴿and Allah helps you with a mighty help﴾ [al-Fath 3], meaning you overpower the enemies with it.

The third is the might of inaccessibility, as said of rare things: "This is 'aziz." As in His saying: ﴿and that is not difficult for Allah﴾ [Ibrahim 20], meaning not unattainable. What is the meaning of inaccessibility as an attribute of Allah? It means that He cannot be affected by any deficiency in His essence or attributes. For this reason the author here says: "invulnerable in His dominion," so no deficiency reaches Him, neither in His essence nor in His attributes.

As for his saying: (﴿The Merciful﴾ toward the people of His obedience), it seems he took this determination from His saying: ﴿and He has always been merciful to the believers﴾ [al-Ahzab 43].

The correct view is that the Merciful is the one who shows mercy to others, and it includes believers and non-believers. But when it is said: ﴿and He has always been merciful to the believers﴾, the intended meaning of the Merciful here is the special Merciful, the special mercy. When it is stated without restriction, He is merciful to all creation. ﴿And whatever blessing you have is from Allah; then when adversity touches you, to Him you cry out﴾ [al-Nahl 53].

Did Allah, mighty and majestic, show mercy to these disbelievers or not? Did Allah show them mercy? Yes, in the general sense He showed them mercy. He sends down rain on them, makes plants grow for them, and gives them provision, health, and other things. But this is general mercy. As for His mercy toward the believers, it is both general and special.

(﴿He who perfected everything He created﴾ [al-Sajdah 7], with the lam vocalized with a fatha as a past verb serving as a description, and with sukun as a badal al-ishtimal (inclusive apposition).) ﴿He who perfected everything He created﴾ is a second canonical reading.

According to the first reading, ﴿perfected everything He created﴾ is a verbal clause describing "everything." According to the second reading, ﴿He who perfected the creation of everything﴾, we say it is badal al-ishtimal, and the meaning is "He who perfected the creation of everything." We have previously explained that the rule for badal al-ishtimal is that it can be correctly made an idafah (genitive construction) to the substituted noun. "Zayd's knowledge benefited me," you say "the knowledge of Zayd benefited me." "Zayd's understanding pleased me," meaning "the understanding of Zayd." "I bought Zayd his garment," meaning "Zayd's garment." This is badal al-ishtimal, since it can be made an idafah to the substituted noun. So here we say ﴿He who perfected everything's creation﴾, meaning He who perfected the creation of everything. The meaning is that He, glorified and exalted, is the Creator, and that everything He created He perfected.

However, this perfection varies. In human beings: ﴿We have certainly created man in the best of stature﴾ [al-Tin 4], ﴿who created you and proportioned you and balanced you﴾ [al-Infitar 7]. So balancing you made you the best form among animals, which is the human being. Yet every thing has a form suited to it, and that form is good relative to it. ﴿And of the grazing livestock are those for burden and those for slaughter﴾ [al-An'am 142]. The hamulah is what is carried upon, and the farsh is what is not carried upon. Everything of this and that has been created in the best and most fitting form for what it was created for (...).

* * *

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. The revelation of the Book﴾ [al-Sajdah 1-2].
* From the benefits of this noble verse: the Noble Qur'an did not come with anything new in the letters that people speak with, yet it rendered them incapable. This is taken from His saying: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim﴾, because the correct view is that they have no meaning.
* And from its benefits: that the Qur'an is the speech of Allah, from His saying: ﴿The revelation of the Book, there is no doubt in it, from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Sajdah 2]. The reason is that the Qur'an is speech, and Allah attributed it to Himself, which requires that it be speech.
* And from it: the affirmation of Allah's elevation, from His saying: ﴿The revelation of the Book, there is no doubt in it, from the Lord of the worlds﴾, and descent can only be from above.
* And from it: the affirmation that the Noble Qur'an is written, from His saying: ﴿the Book﴾. We have previously stated that it is written in the Preserved Tablet, in the scrolls in the hands of the angels, and in the scrolls in our hands.
* And from the benefits of the verse: the emphasis that this Qur'an is sent down from Allah, from His saying: ﴿there is no doubt in it﴾.
* And from its benefits: the affirmation of the lordship of Allah, glorified and exalted, over all creation, from His saying: ﴿from the Lord of the worlds﴾.
* And from its benefits: an indication that this Qur'an binds all people. From where is this taken? From His saying: "its revelation from the Lord of the worlds." If their Lord is the One who sent it down, it means that all of them are obligated to act by this Qur'an.

Then Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿Or do they say, "He has fabricated it"?﴾ [al-Sajdah 3], to the end.
* It is derived from the verse: the demonstration of the audacity of these deniers, from their saying: ﴿He has fabricated it﴾, meaning he invented it and lied.
* And from its benefits: that the Qur'an is truth, not fabricated, from His saying: ﴿Rather, it is the truth﴾.
* And from its benefits: the affirmation of the Messenger's prophethood, may the peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, from His saying: ﴿Rather, it is the truth from your Lord﴾.
* And from its benefits: the care of Allah for His Messenger ﷺ, in that He attributed to him a special lordship. Where is the special lordship? ﴿from your Lord﴾ is this special lordship.
* And from the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of the wisdom in sending down this Qur'an, ﴿that you may warn﴾, because the lam indicates causation.
* And from its benefits: the demonstration of Allah's favor upon those to whom the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, was sent. From where is this taken? From His saying: ﴿no warner has come to them before you﴾ [al-Sajdah 3].
* And from its benefits: the great necessity of sending the Messenger ﷺ. From where do we take it? From the fact that no warner came to them before him, so they are in need of his message. This is according to the view that ma is negative. As for the view that it is a relative pronoun, it is derived from it that the Prophet ﷺ warned of what the prophets before him warned of, and so he is confirming what came before him of the messages.
* And from the benefits of this noble verse: that warning is a cause of guidance, from His saying: ﴿that they may be guided﴾ [al-Sajdah 3]. Reality bears witness to this, for how many a person has been guided by what he was warned of.
* And from the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of Allah's mercy toward creation, in that He sent warners to them for the sake of their guidance.

Then the Exalted said: ﴿Allah is He who created the heavens and the earth and what is between them﴾, to the end [al-Sajdah 4].
* It is derived from this noble verse: that the One who created the heavens is Allah, with no partner. From where is this taken? ﴿Allah is He who created﴾, from the fact that the subject and predicate are both definite, and when the subject and predicate are both definite they indicate restriction: Allah is the One who created, not other than Him.
* And from the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of what this sentence contains of knowledge and power: ﴿Allah is He who created the heavens and the earth﴾, since there is no creating without knowledge and no creating without power. Or not?
* And from its benefits: the demonstration of the greatness of Allah's power. How? Because the creation of these great heavens and earth indicates the greatness of the Creator. Isn't that so? Just as if we saw a lofty palace and a firm building, we would infer from it the greatness of whom? The builder.
* And from the benefits of this noble verse: that between the heavens and the earth there are great signs. From where is this taken?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, but what is the basis for taking it? Because He made it a counterpart to and in contrast with the creation of the heavens and the earth.
* And from its benefits: that the creation of the heavens and the earth was completed in six days, detailed in Surah Fussilat: four for the earth, and two for the heavens.
* And from the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of Allah's elevation, from His saying: ﴿then He istawa upon the Throne﴾, and the Throne is the highest of the created things.
* And from its benefits: the affirmation of Allah's istiwa' upon His Throne, which is His elevation and His settling upon it, without modality (takyif). We do not describe how.
* And from its benefits: the affirmation that voluntary actions subsist in Allah, mighty and majestic.
* A student: The istiwa'.
* The Shaykh: The istiwa' upon the Throne, because it is among the actions He performs by His will, and these are sometimes expressed as the attributes of action (al-sifat al-fi'liyyah).
* And from the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of Allah's greatness and sovereignty, from His saying: ﴿upon the Throne﴾, because the Throne is the seat of kingship, and we have said that the Throne is magnified according to the magnitude of His dominion.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of the Throne (al-'Arsh). What is the Throne? It is the seat of sovereignty. Is it the Kursi (the Footstool) or something else? We say: according to the people of the Sunnah, it is other than the Kursi.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that creation has no protector (waliyy) besides Allah, based on His saying: ﴿You have no protector besides Him, nor any intercessor﴾... [Note: the verse quoted here reads: ﴿Besides Him, you have no protector﴾.]

* Among its benefits: that there is no intercessor for them besides Allah.

* Among its benefits: the refutation of the polytheists' attachment to their deities. Its basis is that if they intend that these be their protectors, helpers, and rescuers from hardship, that will not happen; and if they intend that these be their intercessors, that will not happen either. They say: "We worship them only so that they may bring us near to Allah in closeness." Sometimes they ask them to bring about benefit and avert harm. All of this has no basis for them; rather it is false, since none of that happens except by the permission of Allah: ﴿You have no protector besides Him, nor any intercessor﴾.
So in the verse, as I said, what is this benefit?
* Student: The refutation of the polytheists' attachment...
* The Shaykh: The refutation of the polytheists' attachment to their deities, whether they made them protectors or made them intercessors.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a rebuke of the one who does not remember after this clarification, based on His saying: ﴿Will you not then remember?﴾. This benefit entails another benefit: the obligation to remember the signs of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, so that a person does not pass over them as if they were mere passing words.

Then He said: ﴿He arranges the affair from the heaven to the earth; then it ascends to Him﴾ [As-Sajdah 5].

* In this verse there is evidence of the perfection of Allah's authority, the Exalted: He made the management of affairs belong to whom? To Him. He alone manages, and in this is the perfection of His dominion and that management belongs to Him alone.

* And in it: a refutation of the Qadariyyah, a refutation of the Qadariyyah who claim that a person's affairs are independently his own...

* Student: Because Allah is the One who manages.

* The Shaykh: So, does it contain a refutation of the Qadariyyah? Yes, because we say that the actions of a person are among the matters, and the One who manages them is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
If someone says: "It is also evidence for the view of the Jabriyyah; what do we say?" We say: there are verses showing that a person acts by choice: ﴿for whoever among you wills to go straight. And you do not will except that Allah wills﴾ [At-Takwir 28-29], and His saying: ﴿Among you are those who desire the world, and among you are those who desire the Hereafter﴾ [Ali 'Imran 152], ﴿seeking bounty from their Lord and approval﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 2], and what is similar to that. All of these indicate that a person has will and choice.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of Allah's elevation, the Mighty and Majestic, from His saying: ﴿He arranges the affair from the heaven to the earth; then it ascends to Him﴾ [As-Sajdah 5]. His saying ﴿from the heaven to the earth﴾ is the descent, and ﴿then it ascends to Him﴾ is the ascent. There is no descent except from what is high, and no ascent except to what is high. Thus the elevation of Allah, the Exalted, is derived from both clauses together, each one on its own.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the command of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, encompasses both the heaven and the earth. For if He manages the affair from the heaven to the earth, then the heaven is all the more so. Which of them is closer to you? The heaven.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that this management, which occurs in an instant, descends and ascends in a day whose measure is a thousand years. This occurs in an instant, because Allah says "Be," and it is; and this indicates the perfection of the all-encompassing effect of Allah's will, the Exalted, and that distance does not hinder it.

Then He said: ﴿That is the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, the Mighty, the Merciful﴾ [As-Sajdah 6].

* In this verse: the affirmation of the comprehensiveness of Allah's knowledge, from His saying: ﴿the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾.

* And in it, among its benefits: the affirmation of these two names from the names "the Mighty" and "the Merciful," and the attribute they contain, which is might and mercy. The perfection of His might and mercy, by their combination, is that although He is Mighty, Dominant, and Overpowering, He is also Merciful. For some of the mighty, when they become mighty, do they not show mercy, or not? And some of the merciful, their mercy may reach the point of humility. He, glory be to Him and exalted, combines might and mercy, and this is from His perfection. That is, the combination of might and mercy contains more perfection than the affirmation of might and mercy separately: His mercy is joined with might, not a mercy of humiliation, and His might is joined with mercy, not a might of tyranny devoid of mercy.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 32, verses 7–13 (part 1 of 4):

﴿Who made everything He created good﴾ [al-Sajdah: 7]. There are two readings of it. ﴿Alladhi ahsana kulla shay'in khalaqahu﴾ is read as a past-tense verb, so the clause is a description (sifah) of ﴿shay'in﴾ (thing). Or it is read as ﴿ahsana kulla shay'in khalqahu﴾, in which case it is a substitution of inclusion (badl al-ishtimal, "substitution by inclusion"). We have already given you a rule for recognising badl al-ishtimal: you make the substituted noun an annex (mudaf) to the noun it replaces. In ﴿ahsana kulla shay'in khalqahu﴾, make khalq (creation) an annex to kull shay' (everything), (the One who made the creation of everything good). For example, you say: "Zayd's knowledge benefited me," so you say: "The knowledge of Zayd benefited me," and "I bought Zayd his garment."
* Student: "The garment of Zayd."
* Shaykh: "The garment of Zayd." However, "his garment" could be a substitution by error (badl al-ghalat). He meant to say "I bought the garment of Zayd," but he said "I bought Zayd his garment."
* Student: "Substitution of part (badl al-ba'd)."
* Shaykh: Yes, it works, but that is a part. It is not inclusion. If you say, for example, "I ate the loaf, a third of it," it is correct to say "I ate a third of the loaf."
* Student: The rule (...).
* Shaykh: No, but the difference between them is that that one is a part. This is clear even without making it a rule; it is obvious.
* Student: I was asking (...).
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, the apparent meaning is that it is the lowest heaven, as we said in the tafsir.
* Student: We said: (...) the loftiness of God.
* Shaykh: It is known, because when He is in the heaven He is exalted, and He is above the lowest heaven.
* Student: He manages the affair from the heaven, so the affair proceeds from the heaven.
* Shaykh: Yes, that is so. He passes through the heaven, since He is above the seven heavens; when the command descends, it must pass through the heaven.
* Student: Why did He specify the lowest heaven?
* Shaykh: Because (it is) a thousand years; for if the seventh heaven, for example, were not in that duration, and we take the distance between each heaven and the next to be five hundred years and the diameter of each heaven five hundred years, it would be greater than this.
* Student: (...) returns to the lowest heaven as well.
* Shaykh: It returns to the lowest heaven, passing through it, or then it ascends to Him, to God, with nothing in it; it is not the lowest heaven. Then it ascends to Him, i.e., to God; it is not to (the lower world).
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: It does no harm. And what is the estimate (taqdir)?
* Student: I am asking: if we say a thousand years, we say: it ascends to (...) the height (...).
* Shaykh: No, to God. It ascends to God, to God the Exalted, above the seventh heaven. Or we say it returns to the heaven, because the beginning of the heavens is what faces the earth; it returns to the heaven, passing through it, then it ascends to God, Mighty and Majestic. The point is that what appears is that it is the heaven itself, not the height. When you say "the height," if you mean a specific height, specify it; if you mean an absolute height, then what makes us know that it is (...)? It is not conceivable; it is (...) unless we take the heaven to be only the lowest one.
* Student: The words of the Exalted: ﴿Then He established Himself above the Throne﴾ [al-Sajdah: 4]. There is a hadith that the ratio of the earth and the heavens to the Kursi is that of a ring, and likewise the Kursi relative to the Throne. They will say: the Throne relative to the foot of the Most Merciful is like a ring (...).
* Shaykh: "To the foot of the Most Merciful."
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: I have not heard of it. They say that the Kursi is the place of the two feet. This is established from Ibn 'Abbas. As for the Throne, its measure is known only to God, or none can measure its size except God. This is additional confirmation, but (...).
* * *
﴿He began the creation of man from clay﴾ [al-Sajdah: 7]. ﴿Bada'a﴾ means: He initiated it.
As for the words ﴿khalqa al-insan﴾ (the creation of man): is the intended meaning the genus or a specific individual? The author (al-Mu'allif) followed the view that the intended meaning is a specific individual, i.e., the particular man, Adam: ﴿the creation of man from clay﴾. It may also be that the intended meaning is the genus, ﴿and He began the creation of man﴾, since Adam is one of mankind. God made clear that the beginning of the creation of this man is from clay. There is a difference between His saying ﴿wa bada'a khalqa al-insan﴾ and ﴿khalqa al-insan min tin﴾ (the creation of man from clay), for the latter is clearer in indicating that the intended meaning is a specific person, unlike bada'a. In any case, the verse is open to interpretation: either it is Adam, or the intended meaning is the genus, on the view that it refers to Adam (...).
﴿Then He made his offspring﴾ [al-Sajdah: 8], i.e., the offspring of the man who was originated from clay. ﴿Ja'ala naslahu﴾ (He made his offspring); he says (dhurriyyah, progeny), because nasl means separation, as in His saying: ﴿and they will rush out from every elevation﴾ [al-Anbiya': 96], i.e., they will emerge hastening. So nasl is the progeny, because they issue (nasilah) from their father, i.e., separate from him. ﴿Then He made his offspring from an extract of a liquid, of despised water﴾ [al-Sajdah: 8].
As for His saying ﴿min sulalatin min ma'in﴾ (from an extract of water): ﴿min ma'in﴾ is a description of ﴿sulalah﴾: an extract of water. Strangely, the author explained sulalah as clinging clot ('alaqah), but that is not so. Rather, sulalah is the pure essence of a thing, the essence drawn out from it.
His saying ﴿min sulalatin min ma'in﴾ means: from the pure part of this water. The water, by God's permission, which is semen, contains spermatozoa, from which man is created. This drop is like a container in a saddlebag, meaning that it contains spermatozoa; this is the sulalah.
As for His saying ﴿min sulalatin min ma'in mahin﴾, I told you: to what is it a description? It is a description of "sulalah": this extract is from this water. You may ask: why do you not make ﴿min ma'in mahin﴾ an explanation of ﴿min sulalah﴾, i.e., from an extract which is the despised water? That would be contrary to the apparent meaning. The apparent meaning is that it is an extract from this water. The despised water means weak, which is the drop (nutfah). It is described as weak because it does not flow like water does; it flows slowly, while water flows more strongly. For this reason He said ﴿of despised water﴾, because thick water is not like water that has no thickness.
﴿Then He made his offspring from an extract of despised water (8). Then He proportioned him﴾ [al-Sajdah: 8–9]. If we proceed according to what the author said, there is a great difficulty: it implies that the proportioning of Adam came after making his offspring from despised water. Note this. Is this the reality or the opposite?
* Student: The opposite.
* Shaykh: The opposite; because the proportioning of Adam occurred before his offspring were from despised water. So what is the answer to this?
The answer is in two ways, or one of two ways:
Either it is said that His saying ﴿Then He made his offspring from an extract of despised water﴾ [al-Sajdah: 8] is a parenthetical clause (jumlah mu'taridah) to explain that Adam, who was from clay, had offspring from an extract, then the discourse returns to Adam, so He says: ﴿Then He proportioned him﴾ [al-Sajdah: 9].
Or it is said that this is in the order of mention (tartib dhikri), not in the order of meaning or time.
The order of mention exists in Arabic speech, and among its examples is the poet's words:
"Indeed, whoever ruled, then his father ruled,
then his grandfather ruled after that."
This order is contrary to the reality; yes, this (...).
However, if we say ﴿Then He proportioned him﴾ means the offspring (nasl), as some exegetes said, ﴿and breathed into him of His spirit﴾ [al-Sajdah: 9], then the verse is in the proper sequence and there is no difficulty.
But there is a difficulty with this view, in His saying ﴿and breathed into him of His spirit﴾. This description is specific to whom? It is specific to Adam, as in the hadith: "Moses said to him when he disputed with him: You are the one whom God taught the names of everything, whom He made His angels prostrate to, and into whom He breathed of His spirit." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6614), and Muslim (2652/15), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.] Its apparent meaning is that this is specific to Adam.
For this reason, the first view is better than this view, although this view has strength in terms of the order indicated by "then" (thumma).
But since breathing in the spirit occurred only in Adam and in 'Isa, as you know, this indicates that the intended meaning of His saying ﴿Then He proportioned him﴾ is Adam, and it is a return to the beginning.
﴿And breathed into him of His spirit﴾: the phrase ﴿min ruhih﴾ (of His spirit) is an annex to God. There is a difficulty, since its apparent meaning is that Adam has a portion of God's spirit, so he would be a part of God, and this is impossible and inconceivable. What, then, is the meaning of the annexation?
We say: its meaning is an annexation of creation and honour, as God the Exalted said: ﴿and purify My House for those who circumambulate﴾ [al-Hajj: 26], ﴿My House﴾. Is the Ka'bah a house of God in which He dwells? No, but it is a house which God attributed to Himself as an honour and exaltation.
As God the Exalted said: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mosques of God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 114], and as He said: ﴿the she-camel of God and her drink﴾ [al-Shams: 13]. ﴿The she-camel of God﴾: we said this annexation is for the sake of honouring and exalting this thing.
﴿And breathed into him of His spirit﴾ [al-Sajdah: 9]: i.e., He made him living and sentient after he had been inanimate.
﴿And made for you hearing﴾ [al-Sajdah: 9]. ﴿Ja'ala lakum﴾ (made for you): this is a shift (iltifat) from the third person (ghaybah) to the second person (khitab). ﴿He began the creation of man from clay (7), then made his offspring﴾ [al-Sajdah: 7–8]: all of this is third person. ﴿Then He proportioned him﴾ is third person; ﴿and breathed into him of His spirit﴾ is third person; ﴿and made for you hearing﴾ is second person.
The shift or change (iltifat) is called by the rhetoricians iltifat, and it has a purpose, indeed several purposes. Among them: alerting the addressee. If speech is in a single pattern, no alertness is achieved; but if it varies, alertness occurs, whether the variation is by change of pronouns, as from third person to second or vice versa, or by variation in the intensity of the voice. When a person speaks quietly in one tone, there is no attention; but if he uses a rebuke at times, attention occurs, does it not? Attention occurs. So the shift or change of address achieves attention either way.
﴿And made for you hearing﴾ [al-Sajdah: 9]. He said: ﴿lakum﴾ means for his offspring; the address is undoubtedly to the offspring, as the author said.
* Student: What is the benefit of the shift in it?
* Shaykh: Its benefit is alertness. The benefit depends on the context: for instance, clarification, or increasing the explanation of the blessing, or something similar, depending on the context.
﴿Hearing (al-sam')﴾: the author said it means the faculties of hearing (al-asma'), i.e., "I listen" (astami'), so it is the faculties of hearing. Why did he interpret it as the faculties of hearing? Because ﴿lakum﴾ is an address to a plural, and if the address is to the plural, it must be that each one has hearing, so it becomes plural.
The people of language said: He used the singular for hearing and the plural for sight because sam' is a verbal noun (masdar) of sami'a yasma'u sam'an, and a verbal noun is not made plural or dual; it remains singular, and the intended meaning is the genus.
Al-absar (sights) is the plural of basar, which is the power of sight, and not a verbal noun, because the verbal noun is ibsar (from absara yubsiru ibsaran). So for this reason it is pluralised, and the intended meaning is the genus.
﴿And made for you hearing and sight and hearts﴾ [al-Sajdah: 9].
﴿Al-af'idah﴾ (the hearts) means the hearts. God the Exalted mentioned the means of understanding and the place of understanding. The means of understanding is what? Hearing and sight. The locus of comprehension and awareness is the heart: ﴿made for you hearing and sight﴾. For this reason, hearing and sight are like two channels that pour into the heart: they receive what is heard or seen, then pour into the heart, which is the locus of awareness and perception.
﴿And made for you hearing and sight and hearts﴾, meaning the hearts. Why did He not mention smell, taste, and touch?
Because admonition by the signs occurs through hearing and sight, and He began with hearing because it is more comprehensive and general, for you hear what you do not see. Since it is more comprehensive and general, its affliction is less frequent, thank God. If you compare deafness with blindness, you will find the ratio is small, or not? Because deafness is more severe, so the existence of hearing is more important.
As for His saying ﴿little do you give thanks﴾ [al-Sajdah: 9]: the author says that ﴿qalilan ma﴾, the ma is an extra particle emphasising the paucity: ﴿little do you give thanks﴾.
What is the grammatical status of ﴿qalilan﴾? It is an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq): you give thanks with little thanks, i.e., despite these blessings which God the Mighty and Majestic has enumerated, from the beginning of man's creation, through his movement in the wombs, to his emergence with hearing, sight, and heart, despite these great blessings, the thanks is little, i.e., you give little thanks.
As for this ma, he says it is an extra particle for emphasising paucity. This is well known even now in customary usage: you say "qalilan ma," meaning it emphasises this paucity. So ma is extra? And God knows best (...).
﴿And they said: "When we are lost in the earth, shall we indeed be in a new creation?"﴾ [al-Sajdah: 10].
﴿And they said﴾: the author said: i.e., those who deny the resurrection. They said, presenting this doubt: ﴿When we are lost in the earth, shall we indeed be in a new creation?﴾
﴿When we are lost in the earth﴾: the author said: (we were hidden in it, becoming dust mixed with it). This is the meaning of ﴿dalalna fi al-ard﴾: we were hidden in it and became dust like all other dust. ﴿When﴾ this happens, ﴿shall we indeed be in a new creation?﴾ It is an interrogative of denial: shall we be in a new creation after the earth has consumed us and we have been lost in it?
The interrogative here is one of denial: that is, we will not be that. Is this doubt a valid argument or not?
The answer: it is not a valid argument, because we say: you were created from dust, and the One who created you first from dust is able to return you a second time from this dust, is He not? Yes indeed. For this reason, the verse came after the mention of the creation of man from clay, when He said: ﴿When we are lost in the earth, shall we indeed be in a new creation?﴾ [al-Sajdah: 10].
﴿When we are lost﴾: ("idha") here is conditional; where is its answer? Its answer is understood from the clause after it, meaning: when we are lost in the earth, shall we be brought forth as a new creation?!
As for His saying ﴿shall we indeed be in a new creation?﴾, it means: will it be confirmed that we are in a new creation?
So if someone says: if the interrogative clause here is for denial, how does the particle of emphasis (lam), which indicates confirmation, come in ﴿inna la-fi﴾ (indeed in)?
We say: the meaning is that they deny that this is confirmed: will it be confirmed that we are in a new creation after the earth consumes us, like the words of Joseph's brothers: ﴿They said: "Are you indeed Joseph?" He said: "I am Joseph"﴾ [Yusuf: 90]. The point is that this emphasis is as if they deny what was emphasised, namely that they will return.
﴿Shall we indeed be in a new creation?﴾ [al-Sajdah: 10]. As for His saying ﴿la-fi khalq﴾ (in creation): is "khalq" here used in the sense of "makhluq" (creature)? I.e., shall we indeed be a new nation? Or is it a verbal noun in the sense of determination, i.e., shall we indeed be in creation, that is, that God should create us? Both meanings are possible, and both are correct, and they do not contradict each other. That is: shall we be in a new creation, a new nation? Or shall we be created a new creation after we were lost in the earth and were dust?
The answer: yes, you will be in a new creation, and that is not difficult for God. The One who brought you into being from dust is able to restore you from it, even if the whole human being has perished, although it is related in the hadith that "the whole of him will perish except the coccyx (ajb al-dhanab)," [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4814), and Muslim (2955/142), with his wording, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah], for from it man is created, like the seed of a tree.
Exempted from this are the prophets, peace be upon them, for God forbade the earth to consume the bodies of the prophets. This is evidence of the power of God the Mighty and Majestic. Otherwise, the prophets are human: why? Because they are composed (...)?
* Student: Of dust.
* Shaykh: They were originally created from dust, but now they are of flesh, bone, and skin like all the children of Adam. Nevertheless, the earth does not consume them; it does not consume any part of them at all. As for non-prophets, it consumes them. However, God the Mighty and Majestic may protect the body of some people so that the earth does not consume it, as a kind of honour.
