This is the report of God, Mighty and Majestic, which He does not break. ﴿وَإِنَّهُمْ لَكَاذِبُونَ﴾ "And indeed they are liars" [Al-An'am 27–28].

* Student: Shaykh, but there is a condition here (...) that if they were returned, they would return.
* Shaykh: I do not know. As long as God says this, whatever comes after the words of God is not words. The statement is clear: ﴿وَلَوْ تَرَى إِذْ وُقِفُوا عَلَى النَّارِ ... وَلَوْ رُدُّوا لَعَادُوا لِمَا نُهُوا عَنْهُ﴾.

* Student: And the sinners (*fussaq*)?
* Shaykh: The sinners, no. What is meant is the disbelievers. The sinners do not remain in the Fire forever; they are punished according to their deeds, and then they enter Paradise. The sinners cross the Bridge (*sirat*); they are not taken to the Fire. They cross the Bridge, and then they fall into the Fire according to their deeds.

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: (...) like the Jews and Christians, for example, for whom it does not benefit, since they disbelieved.

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes indeed. Among the present-day atheists, some hold that this worldly life is their only life: they die and live, and that is all, and they have no book or anything. Either he says this out of conviction, or he says it out of imitation and obstinacy.

God, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿وَلَوْ شِئْنَا﴾ "And had We willed" [As-Sajdah 13]. The author says: (The answer to "law" is: you would have seen a dreadful matter), meaning the answer is omitted.

If someone asks: what is the wisdom in omitting the answer? Why is it not mentioned, so that there is no disagreement? And what is the wisdom in the vagueness in His saying: ﴿فَغَشِيَهُمْ مِنَ الْيَمِّ مَا غَشِيَهُمْ﴾ "So the sea covered them, that which covered them" [Ta-Ha 78]? And why is it not mentioned, since it would be clearer?

The answer: in a context of awe-inspiring magnitude (*tahwil*, emphasizing the terrifying gravity of a matter), it is appropriate to leave things vague, so that the mind goes in every direction in magnifying the matter and its dread. For if a thing is named, it may seem less frightening. Suppose someone said to you: "By God, there is a great beast in it that devours people, and does this and that and that," and you were made to dread it, though you have not seen it. You would feel terror. But perhaps when you actually see it, the matter becomes less daunting to you. Likewise, when God leaves such great matters unspecified, they are greater, strike the soul more forcefully, and are more severe and immense. For this reason the response is omitted here, and the enveloping thing is left unspecified in His saying: ﴿Then there covered them of the sea that which covered them﴾. Likewise, *al-Haqqah* and *al-Qari'ah* are left unspecified in such verses as: ﴿The Inevitable Reality. What is the Inevitable Reality? And what will make you know what the Inevitable Reality is?﴾ and ﴿The Striking Calamity. What is the Striking Calamity?﴾ and what is similar to these. All of this is by way of magnification and awe-inspiring emphasis.

He says: ﴿And had We willed, We would have given every soul its guidance﴾ [al-Sajdah 13]. "O Allah, guide us among those whom You have guided." ﴿And had We willed, We would have given every soul its guidance﴾ (so that it would be guided to faith and obedience by its own choice).

As for ﴿had We willed﴾: the pronoun refers to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and He used the plural pronoun as a mark of magnificence. If the Christian says, "The gods are three," and Allah says, ﴿And had We willed﴾ here, [the Christian argues that this is] plural. Produce for us a proof that removes this expression from its meaning; otherwise the truth is with us, and you, O monotheists, are in error. Otherwise, would Allah have said: "And had I willed"?

The answer: this is a case of deception and confusion. Return to His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And your God is One God; there is no deity except Him, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful﴾ [al-Baqarah 163]. How many does that make? One. So ﴿had We willed﴾ is for magnification. ﴿And had We willed﴾ is by way of magnification, and Allah, the Exalted, is great in His attributes. Each of His attributes entails a greatness different from what the other attribute entails, and by the combination of these attributes there is a greater and more exalted majesty.

﴿And had We willed﴾ [al-Sajdah 13]: this is the first answer. ﴿Lā'atayna﴾ means "We would have given." For this reason it takes two objects: the first object is ﴿every soul﴾, and the second is ﴿its guidance﴾. *Al-hudā* means guidance in the sense of indication and success (*tawfiq*). For this reason he said: (so that it would be guided to faith and obedience).

If Allah, the Exalted, had willed, He would have done it, as He said in another verse: ﴿And if your Lord had willed, He would have made mankind one community, but they will continue to differ, except those upon whom your Lord has mercy; and for that He created them﴾ [Hud 118-119]. So if Allah willed, He would have made mankind one community upon faith, monotheism, and steadfastness. But the wisdom of Allah refuses that, for many reasons. Among them: He, the Majestic and Exalted, said to Hell: ﴿I will surely fill Hell with jinn and mankind, all together﴾ [al-Sajdah 13]. ﴿I will surely fill﴾ is an oath and a binding commitment from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, to Hell that He will fill it. ﴿I will surely fill Hell with jinn...﴾

If mankind were one community upon monotheism, would this have come true or not? It would not have come true. Therefore it must come true.

Second: If mankind were one community upon monotheism, would the believer be distinguished from the disbeliever? They would all be one. There would be no trial or test. And if mankind were one community upon monotheism, the enjoining of good and forbidding of evil would be closed off. Why? Because there would be no evil to require forbidding it. And if mankind were one community upon monotheism, would jihad be nullified or not? Whom would we fight? There would be no one.

The point is that there are many wisdoms in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, making people into two categories. For this reason He said here: ﴿But the word from Me has come into effect﴾ [al-Sajdah 13]. ﴿Haqqa﴾ means "became obligatory and established," ﴿al-qawlu﴾ is the subject, and ﴿minnī﴾ is attached to an implied element as a circumstantial qualifier of the word: ﴿But the word has come into effect﴾, issuing ﴿from Me﴾. What is this word? ﴿I will surely fill Hell with jinn and mankind, all together﴾ [al-Sajdah 13]. Here the verb is emphasized with the *nūn* and the *lām* and the implied oath. Is this emphasis grammatically obligatory or not? It is obligatory, because it is an affirmative future oath with no separation between it and its *lām*.

As for His saying ﴿la'amla'anna Jahannam﴾ (I will surely fill Hell): *Jahannam* is one of the names of the Fire. It has been said that it is Arabic, with the *nūn* being extra, and that it is derived from *al-jahm* or *al-tajahhum*, which means darkness. It has also been said that it is an arabized loanword (*mu'arrab*), not Arabic, but arabized. Under all the opinions, what is meant by it is the Fire. We ask Allah for well-being.

﴿I will surely fill Hell with the jinn and mankind﴾ [al-Sajdah 13]: *al-jinnah* means the jinn, and ﴿mankind﴾ means the children of Adam. ﴿All together﴾ means it will be filled with these and those. Which of them is more numerous?

* Students: Allah knows best.
* The Shaykh: Allah knows best. But the apparent division is that they are equal: ﴿from the jinn and mankind﴾.

Do the jinn enter the Fire? It has been understood now from this verse and from another verse that they enter it, as He said: ﴿He will say, "Enter into the Fire among nations that had passed away before you of jinn and men"﴾ [al-A'raf 38]. They enter the Fire. There is a consensus of the Muslims that the disbelieving jinn enter the Fire. Do the believing jinn enter Paradise or not?

The scholars differed about this. The correct view is that they enter Paradise. Allah said: ﴿O assembly of jinn and mankind, did there not come to you messengers from among you, relating to you My verses?...﴾ Then whoever is righteous and reforms, from where? From the jinn and mankind: ﴿Then whoever fears Allah and reforms, there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve. But those who denied Our verses and were arrogant toward them, those are the companions of the Fire, wherein they will abide forever﴾ [al-A'raf 35-36].

He said: ﴿But for he who fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾ [al-Rahman 46], then ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ [al-Rahman 47], addressing whom? The jinn and mankind. This is also evidence that they enter Paradise.

Likewise His saying: ﴿Before them neither man nor jinn has touched them﴾ [al-Rahman 56] indicates that they enter Paradise. This is the view of the majority of the scholars.

Some of them said that they do not enter Paradise, because those who turned back to their people as warners said: ﴿O our people, indeed we have heard a Book revealed after Moses, confirming what was before it, guiding to the truth and to a straight path. O our people, respond to the caller of Allah and believe in him; He will forgive you of your sins and protect you from a painful punishment﴾ [al-Ahqaf 30-31]. They did not say, "He will admit you into Paradise." This indicates that the believer among them is only protected from the painful punishment.

It is said: this is an argument using one text while abandoning other texts. This is not how a person behaves who reconciles the evidences. Furthermore, the station of these people is a station of warning and fear: ﴿They turned back to their people as warners﴾ [al-Ahqaf 29], not as bringers of good tidings (...).

Isn't that so? I think if a cow were made to compete in a contest for a position, would it compete? No, of course not, because that is not its concern. But if fodder were placed in a corner of the house, would it race toward it? Yes, it would race toward it, because Allah guided every creature to what suits it.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the refutation of the theory (...), which is the theory of Darwin, who says that creation arose through evolution and that the origin of man is an ape, which over the length of time became a human. On his principle we do not know what man will become over the length of time. There is no doubt that this theory is false and is disbelief in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. We derive this from His saying: ﴿And He began the creation of man from clay﴾ [al-Sajdah 7]. Nothing is more explicit than this verse: ﴿And He began the creation of man from clay﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the perfection of His power, may He be blessed and exalted, in that He created this wondrous man, in his creation, understanding, management, and intelligence, from this inert thing, which is clay.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of Allah's voluntary acts, which are connected to His will. From where is this derived? From His saying: ﴿And He began﴾, for beginning is from non-existence.

* Among its benefits: that man is originated, having not existed before, from His saying: ﴿And He began﴾.

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Then He made his descendants from an extract of a liquid, despised﴾ [al-Sajdah 8].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that this man who was created from clay has offspring. Offspring was made for him so that this kind of creature would continue, from His saying: ﴿Then He made his descendants﴾.

* Among its benefits: that man is created from semen, from His saying: ﴿his descendants from an extract﴾ [al-Sajdah 8]. *Al-sulālah* is the essence, and *al-mā' al-mahīn* (the despised fluid) is semen. On this basis, he is created from the semen of the man, not the semen of the woman, since the verse says *al-mā' al-mahīn* (the despised fluid).

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the wisdom of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in this fluid, in that He made it of this weakness and this kind, in order to preserve the sperm. For if it were as liquid as water, it would not retain these cells. And if it were thicker than this, it would harm these cells, perhaps killing them. But Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, placed it in this state (...).

Then He said: ﴿Then He proportioned him and breathed into him of His spirit﴾ (to the end of the verse) [al-Sajdah 9].

* It is derived from these noble verses: that Allah, the Exalted, perfected the creation of man, from His saying: ﴿Then He proportioned him﴾. This is supported by His saying: ﴿We have certainly created man in the best of stature﴾ [al-Tin 4], and His saying: ﴿He shaped you and perfected your forms﴾ [Ghafir 64].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that man is a body that is not a human except by the spirit, from His saying: ﴿And breathed into him of His spirit﴾ [al-Sajdah 9].

* Among them (though it is not a strong view): that the spirit is a body, since it is breathed into this perishing body. And indeed the spirit is a body, but a subtle body that is not seen. Yet the angels take it, place it in the funerary spices, and ascend with it to the heaven. But we do not see it when the soul of the dead departs. Do we see anything in him? No, we see nothing.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the demonstration of Allah's blessing upon man in giving him hearing, sight, and hearts, by which he perceives the intelligible. Perceiving the intelligible by what? By hearing and sight. And understanding it? By the heart and its awareness.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that man is little in thanks, from His saying: ﴿Little are you grateful﴾ [al-Sajdah 9]. Just as the grateful are few, and those who fulfill gratitude in the required manner are few. Allah said: ﴿And few of My servants are grateful﴾ [Saba' 13].

* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: The grateful are few because, in terms of individuals and persons, one in ten is grateful, and this is few. The gratitude of the single individual is also little, and the grateful person's gratitude is also little. So His saying ﴿Little are you grateful﴾ [al-Sajdah 9] is in terms of the gratitude of the grateful, while His saying ﴿And few of My servants are grateful﴾ [Saba' 13] is in terms of the number of grateful individuals.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the censure of one who does not give thanks, from His saying: ﴿Little are you grateful﴾ [al-Sajdah 9].

* Among its benefits: that a person should make his gratitude proportionate to the blessing. In the case of hearing, he uses his hearing for what brings him closer to Allah, and restrains it from what Allah has forbidden. Likewise with sight. As for the heart, it is obligatory upon it to turn away from everything Allah has forbidden, and to turn toward everything Allah has commanded.

Then the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And they say, "When we are lost in the earth, will we indeed be in a new creation?"﴾ [al-Sajdah 10].

* Derived from this noble verse: the rebuke of these deniers, as will come at its end: ﴿Rather, they are disbelievers in the meeting with their Lord﴾ [al-Sajdah 10].

* Among its benefits: that these deniers were doubtful about the power of Allah, from their saying: ﴿When we are lost﴾ and ﴿will we indeed be﴾.
It is possible that this was obstinacy on their part, and that they knew the power of Allah but were stubborn. This is supported by His saying: ﴿Rather, they are disbelievers in the meeting with their Lord﴾, meaning the matter is clear, but these are disbelievers.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the perfection of Allah's power, the Mighty and Majestic, in restoring the dead after they had vanished into the earth and dissolved in it, Allah bringing them forth as a new creation.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the refutation of the saying of one who says that resurrection is bringing into existence from non-existence. For there are those who say that this creation is totally annihilated and then brought into being anew. This view is false, because if it were so, reward would be for one who did not act, and punishment for one who did not act. If we say he is annihilated completely and then a new creation arises and is held to account, this new one is not the original, so he would be punished for what he did not do and rewarded for what he did not do. Allah, the Exalted, has made clear that the person himself is what is restored. He is not annihilated and then created anew, but he is restored: ﴿As We began the first creation, We will repeat it﴾ [al-Anbiya' 104]. He did not say, "We will create another." The evidence is His saying: ﴿When we are lost in the earth, will we indeed be in a new creation?﴾ [al-Sajdah 10]. ("When we are lost": they say, "How, after we are hidden in the earth and become dust, will we be resurrected?") This shows that resurrection is the restoration of what previously existed, not the beginning of a new creation.

* Among the benefits of the verse: that these deniers of resurrection have no proof except mere disbelief, from His saying: ﴿Rather, they are disbelievers in the meeting with their Lord﴾ [al-Sajdah 10].

* Among its benefits: the affirmation of meeting Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, on the Day of Resurrection, from His saying: ﴿meeting﴾. Similar to it is His saying: ﴿O mankind, indeed you are laboring toward your Lord with labor, and you will meet Him﴾ [al-Inshiqaq 6].

He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Say, "The angel of death who has been charged with you will take your souls"﴾ (to the end) [al-Sajdah 11].

* It is derived from this noble verse: that the one who takes charge of seizing souls is the Angel of Death, from His saying: ﴿Say, "The Angel of Death will take you"﴾.

* Among its benefits: the affirmation of the angels, from His saying: ﴿the Angel of Death﴾. The angels are an unseen realm whom Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, created from light, and made them listeners and obedient to Him, and empowered them to carry out what is commanded, from His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And those near Him are not too proud to worship Him, nor do they tire. They glorify Him night and day; they do not slacken﴾ [al-Anbiya' 19-20]. And He, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Over it are angels, harsh and severe, who do not disobey Allah in what He commands them, and do what they are commanded﴾ [al-Tahrim 6], as an indication of perfect compliance and perfect power.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the perfection of Allah's arrangement of affairs and the precision of His management of them, from His saying: ﴿who has been charged with you﴾, for every angel is assigned to something with complete order, precision, and excellence.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the greatness of Allah's sovereignty. From where is this derived? From His saying: ﴿who has been charged with you﴾. We have already mentioned in the lesson that this entrusting is not a sign of incapacity on the part of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, but is to demonstrate His sovereignty and greatness.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of return to Allah: ﴿Then to your Lord you will be returned﴾ [al-Sajdah 11].
From it is derived the affirmation of recompense, because this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿Then to your Lord you will be returned﴾.

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿If you could but see when the criminals will bow their heads before their Lord﴾ (to the end) [al-Sajdah 12].

This is a statement of the horror of what will befall the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection. From where is this derived? From His saying: ﴿If you could but see﴾, and its implied response is: "you would see a dreadful matter."

* Among its benefits: these criminals who were arrogant and held their heads high in the world will, on the Day of Resurrection, be in the opposite state, as Allah says: ﴿Hanging down their heads﴾. The author says: "(out of shame)", but the correct meaning is: humiliation, disgrace and shame, and we seek refuge in Allah.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the criminals on the Day of Resurrection will acknowledge the truth. From where do we derive this? ﴿Our Lord, we have seen and heard﴾ [As-Sajdah 12]. But will this benefit them? No. After a person has witnessed the punishment or the recompense, this acknowledgment will not benefit him on that Day.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: these people seek to return to the world, as Allah says: ﴿So send us back, we will act righteously﴾ [As-Sajdah 12].
From this it follows that the Hereafter may contain some acts of worship, because supplication is a form of worship, and they are calling upon Allah.
Accordingly, whoever denies that the Hereafter is an abode of obligation (taklif) or an abode of action, his denial in a general sense is clearly open to objection, for the Hereafter may contain obligation: ﴿On the Day when the shin will be uncovered, and they will be called to prostration﴾ [al-Qalam 42]. ﴿They will be called﴾: is this an obligation or not? It is an obligation. So the Hereafter may contain obligation.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: these deniers are certain of the matter of the Hereafter, as Allah says: ﴿Indeed, we are certain﴾ [As-Sajdah 12].

* Among its benefits: their acknowledgment against themselves that their previous deeds were not correct. From where? From His saying: ﴿we will act righteously﴾ [As-Sajdah 12], meaning: it is as if at first they were not doing righteous deeds.

Then Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And if We had willed, We would have given every soul its guidance, but the word from Me has come into effect﴾ to the end [As-Sajdah 13].

* From this noble verse is derived: the affirmation of Allah's will, by His saying: ﴿And if We had willed﴾.

* Among its benefits: the completeness of His authority. He said: ﴿And if We had willed, We would have given every soul its guidance﴾.

* Among its benefits also: the affirmation of His wisdom, in that He did not give every soul its guidance. We have previously mentioned some of the wisdoms regarding the difference among people into believers and disbelievers.

* From this noble verse is derived: the refutation of the Qadariyyah (the sect that denies Allah's predestination of human actions). Who are the Qadariyyah?
The Qadariyyah are those who say: a human being is independent in his deeds; Allah the Exalted has no decree or creation in them. He wills for himself and acts by himself, with no connection to Allah in his action. These are the Qadariyyah, and His saying: ﴿And if We had willed, We would have given﴾ refutes them.
But does the verse contain evidence for the matter of the Jabriyyah (the sect that denies human choice and says man is compelled)? Its apparent meaning might, but other verses show that they have no proof in it, because Allah the Exalted gave man power and choice. We, the People of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah), do not take some of the Book and leave out some; rather we take the whole Book. We believe that Allah's will is above everything, and we believe that man has a will, a determination and the power to act, and that man is the doer, and it is not Allah who is the doer.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of Allah's speech, that Allah speaks, by His saying: ﴿The word from Me has come into effect, that I will surely fill﴾ [As-Sajdah 13].

* Among its benefits: that His speech, glorified and exalted is He, is with letters, because His saying: ﴿I will surely fill﴾ consists of letters, or not? It consists of letters, so Allah's speech is with letters.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the refutation of those who claim that Allah's speech is the meaning subsisting in the self (al-ma'na al-qa'im bil-nafs), for if it were so, He would have said, glorified and exalted is He: "But I wished to fill it." He did not say: ﴿But the word from Me has come into effect, that I will surely fill﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of the Fire, by His saying: ﴿I will surely fill Hell﴾.

* Among its benefits: that Allah, majestic and exalted, fulfils His promises to those He made covenants with. Where? He promised the Fire that He would fill it, and He fulfilled to it what He promised it. For this reason Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And who is more faithful to his covenant than Allah?﴾ [At-Tawbah 111], and He the Exalted said: ﴿And fulfil My covenant, I will fulfil your covenant﴾ [Al-Baqarah 40].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the jinn enter the Fire. From where? ﴿Of the jinn and mankind, all together﴾ [As-Sajdah 13].
As for whether they enter Paradise: it has previously been mentioned that there is a difference of opinion on this, and that the correct view is that they do enter it, and we have explained the evidence for this from the Qur'an.

We now begin a new lesson.

* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: This was mentioned by the Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him (...), and it has been reported from some of the early Muslims (salaf), but there is no evidence for it (...).
* Student: Does obligation in the Hereafter carry reward?
* The Shaykh: Yes. For this reason, the people of the interval (ahl al-fatrah, those who lived between prophets and never received a message) will be held to obligation in the Hereafter: whoever of them obeys enters Paradise, and whoever disobeys enters the Fire.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: (...) for ordering. "Then He istawa (rose) over the Throne after creating the heavens" — but before He created the heaven, what (...). At the time of creation He was not yet istawa, and after creation He is istawa. As for before that, Allah knows best.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 32, verses 7–13 (part 1 of 4):

﴿Who made everything He created good﴾ [al-Sajdah: 7]. There are two readings of it. ﴿Alladhi ahsana kulla shay'in khalaqahu﴾ is read as a past-tense verb, so the clause is a description (sifah) of ﴿shay'in﴾ (thing). Or it is read as ﴿ahsana kulla shay'in khalqahu﴾, in which case it is a substitution of inclusion (badl al-ishtimal, "substitution by inclusion"). We have already given you a rule for recognising badl al-ishtimal: you make the substituted noun an annex (mudaf) to the noun it replaces. In ﴿ahsana kulla shay'in khalqahu﴾, make khalq (creation) an annex to kull shay' (everything), (the One who made the creation of everything good). For example, you say: "Zayd's knowledge benefited me," so you say: "The knowledge of Zayd benefited me," and "I bought Zayd his garment."
* Student: "The garment of Zayd."
* Shaykh: "The garment of Zayd." However, "his garment" could be a substitution by error (badl al-ghalat). He meant to say "I bought the garment of Zayd," but he said "I bought Zayd his garment."
* Student: "Substitution of part (badl al-ba'd)."
* Shaykh: Yes, it works, but that is a part. It is not inclusion. If you say, for example, "I ate the loaf, a third of it," it is correct to say "I ate a third of the loaf."
* Student: The rule (...).
* Shaykh: No, but the difference between them is that that one is a part. This is clear even without making it a rule; it is obvious.
* Student: I was asking (...).
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, the apparent meaning is that it is the lowest heaven, as we said in the tafsir.
* Student: We said: (...) the loftiness of God.
* Shaykh: It is known, because when He is in the heaven He is exalted, and He is above the lowest heaven.
* Student: He manages the affair from the heaven, so the affair proceeds from the heaven.
* Shaykh: Yes, that is so. He passes through the heaven, since He is above the seven heavens; when the command descends, it must pass through the heaven.
* Student: Why did He specify the lowest heaven?
* Shaykh: Because (it is) a thousand years; for if the seventh heaven, for example, were not in that duration, and we take the distance between each heaven and the next to be five hundred years and the diameter of each heaven five hundred years, it would be greater than this.
* Student: (...) returns to the lowest heaven as well.
* Shaykh: It returns to the lowest heaven, passing through it, or then it ascends to Him, to God, with nothing in it; it is not the lowest heaven. Then it ascends to Him, i.e., to God; it is not to (the lower world).
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: It does no harm. And what is the estimate (taqdir)?
* Student: I am asking: if we say a thousand years, we say: it ascends to (...) the height (...).
* Shaykh: No, to God. It ascends to God, to God the Exalted, above the seventh heaven. Or we say it returns to the heaven, because the beginning of the heavens is what faces the earth; it returns to the heaven, passing through it, then it ascends to God, Mighty and Majestic. The point is that what appears is that it is the heaven itself, not the height. When you say "the height," if you mean a specific height, specify it; if you mean an absolute height, then what makes us know that it is (...)? It is not conceivable; it is (...) unless we take the heaven to be only the lowest one.
* Student: The words of the Exalted: ﴿Then He established Himself above the Throne﴾ [al-Sajdah: 4]. There is a hadith that the ratio of the earth and the heavens to the Kursi is that of a ring, and likewise the Kursi relative to the Throne. They will say: the Throne relative to the foot of the Most Merciful is like a ring (...).
* Shaykh: "To the foot of the Most Merciful."
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: I have not heard of it. They say that the Kursi is the place of the two feet. This is established from Ibn 'Abbas. As for the Throne, its measure is known only to God, or none can measure its size except God. This is additional confirmation, but (...).
* * *
﴿He began the creation of man from clay﴾ [al-Sajdah: 7]. ﴿Bada'a﴾ means: He initiated it.
As for the words ﴿khalqa al-insan﴾ (the creation of man): is the intended meaning the genus or a specific individual? The author (al-Mu'allif) followed the view that the intended meaning is a specific individual, i.e., the particular man, Adam: ﴿the creation of man from clay﴾. It may also be that the intended meaning is the genus, ﴿and He began the creation of man﴾, since Adam is one of mankind. God made clear that the beginning of the creation of this man is from clay. There is a difference between His saying ﴿wa bada'a khalqa al-insan﴾ and ﴿khalqa al-insan min tin﴾ (the creation of man from clay), for the latter is clearer in indicating that the intended meaning is a specific person, unlike bada'a. In any case, the verse is open to interpretation: either it is Adam, or the intended meaning is the genus, on the view that it refers to Adam (...).
﴿Then He made his offspring﴾ [al-Sajdah: 8], i.e., the offspring of the man who was originated from clay. ﴿Ja'ala naslahu﴾ (He made his offspring); he says (dhurriyyah, progeny), because nasl means separation, as in His saying: ﴿and they will rush out from every elevation﴾ [al-Anbiya': 96], i.e., they will emerge hastening. So nasl is the progeny, because they issue (nasilah) from their father, i.e., separate from him. ﴿Then He made his offspring from an extract of a liquid, of despised water﴾ [al-Sajdah: 8].
As for His saying ﴿min sulalatin min ma'in﴾ (from an extract of water): ﴿min ma'in﴾ is a description of ﴿sulalah﴾: an extract of water. Strangely, the author explained sulalah as clinging clot ('alaqah), but that is not so. Rather, sulalah is the pure essence of a thing, the essence drawn out from it.
His saying ﴿min sulalatin min ma'in﴾ means: from the pure part of this water. The water, by God's permission, which is semen, contains spermatozoa, from which man is created. This drop is like a container in a saddlebag, meaning that it contains spermatozoa; this is the sulalah.
As for His saying ﴿min sulalatin min ma'in mahin﴾, I told you: to what is it a description? It is a description of "sulalah": this extract is from this water. You may ask: why do you not make ﴿min ma'in mahin﴾ an explanation of ﴿min sulalah﴾, i.e., from an extract which is the despised water? That would be contrary to the apparent meaning. The apparent meaning is that it is an extract from this water. The despised water means weak, which is the drop (nutfah). It is described as weak because it does not flow like water does; it flows slowly, while water flows more strongly. For this reason He said ﴿of despised water﴾, because thick water is not like water that has no thickness.
﴿Then He made his offspring from an extract of despised water (8). Then He proportioned him﴾ [al-Sajdah: 8–9]. If we proceed according to what the author said, there is a great difficulty: it implies that the proportioning of Adam came after making his offspring from despised water. Note this. Is this the reality or the opposite?
* Student: The opposite.
* Shaykh: The opposite; because the proportioning of Adam occurred before his offspring were from despised water. So what is the answer to this?
The answer is in two ways, or one of two ways:
Either it is said that His saying ﴿Then He made his offspring from an extract of despised water﴾ [al-Sajdah: 8] is a parenthetical clause (jumlah mu'taridah) to explain that Adam, who was from clay, had offspring from an extract, then the discourse returns to Adam, so He says: ﴿Then He proportioned him﴾ [al-Sajdah: 9].
Or it is said that this is in the order of mention (tartib dhikri), not in the order of meaning or time.
The order of mention exists in Arabic speech, and among its examples is the poet's words:
"Indeed, whoever ruled, then his father ruled,
then his grandfather ruled after that."
This order is contrary to the reality; yes, this (...).
However, if we say ﴿Then He proportioned him﴾ means the offspring (nasl), as some exegetes said, ﴿and breathed into him of His spirit﴾ [al-Sajdah: 9], then the verse is in the proper sequence and there is no difficulty.
But there is a difficulty with this view, in His saying ﴿and breathed into him of His spirit﴾. This description is specific to whom? It is specific to Adam, as in the hadith: "Moses said to him when he disputed with him: You are the one whom God taught the names of everything, whom He made His angels prostrate to, and into whom He breathed of His spirit." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6614), and Muslim (2652/15), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.] Its apparent meaning is that this is specific to Adam.
For this reason, the first view is better than this view, although this view has strength in terms of the order indicated by "then" (thumma).
But since breathing in the spirit occurred only in Adam and in 'Isa, as you know, this indicates that the intended meaning of His saying ﴿Then He proportioned him﴾ is Adam, and it is a return to the beginning.
﴿And breathed into him of His spirit﴾: the phrase ﴿min ruhih﴾ (of His spirit) is an annex to God. There is a difficulty, since its apparent meaning is that Adam has a portion of God's spirit, so he would be a part of God, and this is impossible and inconceivable. What, then, is the meaning of the annexation?
We say: its meaning is an annexation of creation and honour, as God the Exalted said: ﴿and purify My House for those who circumambulate﴾ [al-Hajj: 26], ﴿My House﴾. Is the Ka'bah a house of God in which He dwells? No, but it is a house which God attributed to Himself as an honour and exaltation.
As God the Exalted said: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mosques of God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 114], and as He said: ﴿the she-camel of God and her drink﴾ [al-Shams: 13]. ﴿The she-camel of God﴾: we said this annexation is for the sake of honouring and exalting this thing.
﴿And breathed into him of His spirit﴾ [al-Sajdah: 9]: i.e., He made him living and sentient after he had been inanimate.
﴿And made for you hearing﴾ [al-Sajdah: 9]. ﴿Ja'ala lakum﴾ (made for you): this is a shift (iltifat) from the third person (ghaybah) to the second person (khitab). ﴿He began the creation of man from clay (7), then made his offspring﴾ [al-Sajdah: 7–8]: all of this is third person. ﴿Then He proportioned him﴾ is third person; ﴿and breathed into him of His spirit﴾ is third person; ﴿and made for you hearing﴾ is second person.
The shift or change (iltifat) is called by the rhetoricians iltifat, and it has a purpose, indeed several purposes. Among them: alerting the addressee. If speech is in a single pattern, no alertness is achieved; but if it varies, alertness occurs, whether the variation is by change of pronouns, as from third person to second or vice versa, or by variation in the intensity of the voice. When a person speaks quietly in one tone, there is no attention; but if he uses a rebuke at times, attention occurs, does it not? Attention occurs. So the shift or change of address achieves attention either way.
﴿And made for you hearing﴾ [al-Sajdah: 9]. He said: ﴿lakum﴾ means for his offspring; the address is undoubtedly to the offspring, as the author said.
* Student: What is the benefit of the shift in it?
* Shaykh: Its benefit is alertness. The benefit depends on the context: for instance, clarification, or increasing the explanation of the blessing, or something similar, depending on the context.
﴿Hearing (al-sam')﴾: the author said it means the faculties of hearing (al-asma'), i.e., "I listen" (astami'), so it is the faculties of hearing. Why did he interpret it as the faculties of hearing? Because ﴿lakum﴾ is an address to a plural, and if the address is to the plural, it must be that each one has hearing, so it becomes plural.
The people of language said: He used the singular for hearing and the plural for sight because sam' is a verbal noun (masdar) of sami'a yasma'u sam'an, and a verbal noun is not made plural or dual; it remains singular, and the intended meaning is the genus.
Al-absar (sights) is the plural of basar, which is the power of sight, and not a verbal noun, because the verbal noun is ibsar (from absara yubsiru ibsaran). So for this reason it is pluralised, and the intended meaning is the genus.
﴿And made for you hearing and sight and hearts﴾ [al-Sajdah: 9].
﴿Al-af'idah﴾ (the hearts) means the hearts. God the Exalted mentioned the means of understanding and the place of understanding. The means of understanding is what? Hearing and sight. The locus of comprehension and awareness is the heart: ﴿made for you hearing and sight﴾. For this reason, hearing and sight are like two channels that pour into the heart: they receive what is heard or seen, then pour into the heart, which is the locus of awareness and perception.
﴿And made for you hearing and sight and hearts﴾, meaning the hearts. Why did He not mention smell, taste, and touch?
Because admonition by the signs occurs through hearing and sight, and He began with hearing because it is more comprehensive and general, for you hear what you do not see. Since it is more comprehensive and general, its affliction is less frequent, thank God. If you compare deafness with blindness, you will find the ratio is small, or not? Because deafness is more severe, so the existence of hearing is more important.
As for His saying ﴿little do you give thanks﴾ [al-Sajdah: 9]: the author says that ﴿qalilan ma﴾, the ma is an extra particle emphasising the paucity: ﴿little do you give thanks﴾.
What is the grammatical status of ﴿qalilan﴾? It is an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq): you give thanks with little thanks, i.e., despite these blessings which God the Mighty and Majestic has enumerated, from the beginning of man's creation, through his movement in the wombs, to his emergence with hearing, sight, and heart, despite these great blessings, the thanks is little, i.e., you give little thanks.
As for this ma, he says it is an extra particle for emphasising paucity. This is well known even now in customary usage: you say "qalilan ma," meaning it emphasises this paucity. So ma is extra? And God knows best (...).
﴿And they said: "When we are lost in the earth, shall we indeed be in a new creation?"﴾ [al-Sajdah: 10].
﴿And they said﴾: the author said: i.e., those who deny the resurrection. They said, presenting this doubt: ﴿When we are lost in the earth, shall we indeed be in a new creation?﴾
﴿When we are lost in the earth﴾: the author said: (we were hidden in it, becoming dust mixed with it). This is the meaning of ﴿dalalna fi al-ard﴾: we were hidden in it and became dust like all other dust. ﴿When﴾ this happens, ﴿shall we indeed be in a new creation?﴾ It is an interrogative of denial: shall we be in a new creation after the earth has consumed us and we have been lost in it?
The interrogative here is one of denial: that is, we will not be that. Is this doubt a valid argument or not?
The answer: it is not a valid argument, because we say: you were created from dust, and the One who created you first from dust is able to return you a second time from this dust, is He not? Yes indeed. For this reason, the verse came after the mention of the creation of man from clay, when He said: ﴿When we are lost in the earth, shall we indeed be in a new creation?﴾ [al-Sajdah: 10].
﴿When we are lost﴾: ("idha") here is conditional; where is its answer? Its answer is understood from the clause after it, meaning: when we are lost in the earth, shall we be brought forth as a new creation?!
As for His saying ﴿shall we indeed be in a new creation?﴾, it means: will it be confirmed that we are in a new creation?
So if someone says: if the interrogative clause here is for denial, how does the particle of emphasis (lam), which indicates confirmation, come in ﴿inna la-fi﴾ (indeed in)?
We say: the meaning is that they deny that this is confirmed: will it be confirmed that we are in a new creation after the earth consumes us, like the words of Joseph's brothers: ﴿They said: "Are you indeed Joseph?" He said: "I am Joseph"﴾ [Yusuf: 90]. The point is that this emphasis is as if they deny what was emphasised, namely that they will return.
﴿Shall we indeed be in a new creation?﴾ [al-Sajdah: 10]. As for His saying ﴿la-fi khalq﴾ (in creation): is "khalq" here used in the sense of "makhluq" (creature)? I.e., shall we indeed be a new nation? Or is it a verbal noun in the sense of determination, i.e., shall we indeed be in creation, that is, that God should create us? Both meanings are possible, and both are correct, and they do not contradict each other. That is: shall we be in a new creation, a new nation? Or shall we be created a new creation after we were lost in the earth and were dust?
The answer: yes, you will be in a new creation, and that is not difficult for God. The One who brought you into being from dust is able to restore you from it, even if the whole human being has perished, although it is related in the hadith that "the whole of him will perish except the coccyx (ajb al-dhanab)," [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4814), and Muslim (2955/142), with his wording, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah], for from it man is created, like the seed of a tree.
Exempted from this are the prophets, peace be upon them, for God forbade the earth to consume the bodies of the prophets. This is evidence of the power of God the Mighty and Majestic. Otherwise, the prophets are human: why? Because they are composed (...)?
* Student: Of dust.
* Shaykh: They were originally created from dust, but now they are of flesh, bone, and skin like all the children of Adam. Nevertheless, the earth does not consume them; it does not consume any part of them at all. As for non-prophets, it consumes them. However, God the Mighty and Majestic may protect the body of some people so that the earth does not consume it, as a kind of honour.
* Student: Always?
* Shaykh: What is the meaning of "always"?
* Student: That means (...) the prophets?
* Shaykh: That is the rule: that it (...).
﴿Shall we indeed be in a new creation?﴾: no, there is a reading in it, with the two hamzahs made clear, the second softened, and an alif inserted between them, in both ways, in both places (...).

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on Surah 32, verses 7–13 (part 2 of 4)**

Pronouncing both hamzas in full in both places, so it is read: ﴿أَإِذَا ضَلَلْنَا فِي الْأَرْضِ أَإِنَّا لَفِي خَلْقٍ جَدِيدٍ﴾ (Are we, when we have gone astray in the earth, truly in a new creation?). This is the first reading, *tahqiq* (full pronunciation of the hamza).

Inserting an alif between two fully pronounced hamzas: ﴿آإِذَا ضَلَلْنَا فِي الْأَرْضِ آإِنَّا لَفِي خَلْقٍ جَدِيدٍ﴾. How many readings are there here? Two readings.

Easing the second hamza (*tas-hil*): ﴿أَاِذَا ضَلَلْنَا فِي الْأَرْضِ﴾ with the second hamza not fully pronounced, but placed between the hamza and the ya, without an alif.

With an alif, without making the two hamzas clear: ﴿آاِذَا﴾ with the second hamza placed between the hamza and the ya. So the readings are four.

﴿أَإِذَا ضَلَلْنَا فِي الْأَرْضِ﴾. The author, may God Most High have mercy on him, says: (God Most High said: ﴿بَلْ هُمْ بِلِقَاءِ رَبِّهِمْ﴾ "Rather, they are in denial of the meeting with their Lord", i.e. the resurrection, ﴿كَافِرُونَ﴾ "they disbelieve.") Is the word "bal" (rather) here for *al-ibtali* (refutation) or for *al-intiqali* (transition)? For refutation. Meaning: the matter is not as they liken and confuse it. They know God's power, but they deny it: ﴿بَلْ هُمْ بِلِقَاءِ رَبِّهِمْ كَافِرُونَ﴾ [As-Sajdah 10].

His saying ﴿بِلِقَاءِ رَبِّهِمْ﴾ is connected to ﴿كَافِرُونَ﴾. ﴿كَافِرُونَ﴾ is the predicate of the subject ﴿هُمْ﴾ (predicate of the subject: *khabar al-mubtada'*). That is: rather, they disbelieve in the meeting with their Lord, or in encountering Him. When does the encounter happen? It happens at the resurrection. Whoever disbelieves in meeting God has disbelieved in God. This is why the author, explaining it by its meaning rather than its wording, said: (by the resurrection). Otherwise it is more specific than the resurrection.

"Liqa'" means "meeting" (*mulaqah*): ﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الْإِنسَانُ إِنَّكَ كَادِحٌ إِلَى رَبِّكَ كَدْحًا فَمُلَاقِيهِ﴾ "O mankind, indeed you are labouring toward your Lord with great exertion, and you will meet Him" [Al-Inshiqaq 6]. "Al-insan" means any human being: ﴿فَأَمَّا مَنْ أُوتِيَ كِتَابَهُ بِيَمِينِهِ﴾ "As for he who is given his record in his right hand" [Al-Inshiqaq 7], and so on. That is, these are the ones who disbelieve in the meeting with God, because they do not believe in the resurrection, and whoever does not believe in the resurrection does not believe in the meeting with God.

Then He, Most High, said: (Say, ﴿قُلْ﴾, to them: ﴿يَتَوَفَّاكُمْ مَلَكُ الْمَوْتِ الَّذِي وُكِّلَ بِكُمْ﴾ "The angel of death who has been entrusted with you will take you [in death]" [As-Sajdah 11], i.e. by seizing your souls.)

﴿يَتَوَفَّاكُمْ﴾ means "he takes you," i.e. seizes you. As you say: "I took (*tawaffaytu*) my right from so-and-so," meaning I seized it, and similarly "I collected it in full" (*istawfaytu*), meaning I seized it completely, and completeness is the meaning of *wafa'*.

So the meaning of ﴿يَتَوَفَّاكُمْ﴾ is: he seizes you, and what is meant is the seizing of souls.

His saying ﴿مَلَكُ الْمَوْتِ﴾: *malak* is the singular of *mala'ikah* (angels), or the singular of *amlak*. It is derived from *al-alukah*, meaning "message." Accordingly, its original form is *ma'lak*, then it was transposed: the lam was moved forward and the hamza backward, becoming *mal'ak*, then it was lightened by dropping the hamza, becoming *malak*. This is why, when it is made plural, the hamza returns: *mala'ikah*, and one does not say *ma'ahikah*, because it has undergone *i'lal bil-tahwil* (morphological alteration by transposition), that is, it has been moved forward and backward. It derives from *al-alukah*, i.e. the message.

So ﴿مَلَكُ الْمَوْتِ﴾ means: the one who has been sent. God, may He be Mighty and Majestic, sent him to seize souls, as He said in another verse: ﴿تَوَفَّتْهُ رُسُلُنَا وَهُمْ لَا يُفَرِّطُونَ﴾ "Our messengers take him, and they do not neglect" [Al-An'am 61].

His saying ﴿مَلَكُ الْمَوْتِ﴾ is in construct form with "death," because he causes people to die by God's permission. So he is called "the angel of death." He has been named in some traditions (*al-athar*) as 'Azra'il, but that has not been authenticated from the Messenger of God ﷺ.

It has already been mentioned that the angels whose names are authenticated are Jibril, Mika'il and Israfil; Malik, keeper of the Fire; and Ridwan, keeper of Paradise. Munkar and Nakir are somewhat uncertain, and some have denied them.

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: (...) some have denied it. In any case, 'Azra'il is not established from the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, although this name is the most famous name of the angels among the common people.

His saying ﴿مَلَكُ الْمَوْتِ الَّذِي وُكِّلَ بِكُمْ﴾ [As-Sajdah 11]: who entrusted him? God, Mighty and Majestic, entrusted him. This entrusting is not an entrusting out of need, but an entrusting of sovereignty and greatness, because the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, has no need of anyone to help Him. His entrusting the angels with things is not out of need. When I entrust someone, I may be in need of it, because I cannot carry out the work directly. But the Lord, glorified and exalted, has no need. When He wills a thing, He says to it "Be," and it is. Yet He entrusts this as an entrusting of sovereignty and greatness, to show His authority and majesty, and that everything is in His service, glorified and exalted, and in His worship.

His saying ﴿الَّذِي وُكِّلَ بِكُمْ﴾ [As-Sajdah 11] means: God has entrusted him. So God is both one who entrusts (*wakil*) and one who is entrusted? ﴿وَكَفَى بِاللَّهِ وَكِيلًا﴾ "And God is sufficient as a trustee" [An-Nisa' 81]. As for the one who entrusts: ﴿فَقَدْ وَكَّلْنَا بِهَا قَوْمًا﴾ "We have entrusted it to a people" [Al-An'am 89]. Here He says ﴿الَّذِي وُكِّلَ بِكُمْ﴾ [As-Sajdah 11]. But His being a trustee does not mean that He is entrusted by another, with a higher entrusting party, as is customary among creatures. Rather, He is a trustee in the sense of being a watcher over His servants, dominating over them.

His saying, glorified and exalted, ﴿يَتَوَفَّاكُمْ مَلَكُ الْمَوْتِ﴾ [As-Sajdah 11], here in the singular: ﴿يَتَوَفَّاكُمْ مَلَكُ﴾. In another verse, in a general context: ﴿حَتَّى إِذَا جَاءَ أَحَدَكُمُ الْمَوْتُ تَوَفَّتْهُ رُسُلُنَا﴾ "Until, when death comes to one of you, Our messengers take him" [Al-An'am 61], in the plural. And in another verse: ﴿اللَّهُ يَتَوَفَّى الْأَنْفُسَ حِينَ مَوْتِهَا﴾ "God takes the souls at the time of their death" [Az-Zumar 42], in Az-Zumar. So how do we reconcile these three verses?

The scholars have reconciled them by saying: His saying ﴿اللَّهُ يَتَوَفَّى الْأَنْفُسَ﴾ [Az-Zumar 42] is the origin, that the one who takes is God, because He is the Disposer. The disposer of a thing is its doer, as you say: "the king built a palace," meaning he went and fetched the basket, the spade, the hoe and the bucket of water, mixed the mud and began carrying it on his back and building? Is it not so?

* Students: No.
* Shaykh: Is the matter not so?
* Students: No.
* Shaykh: So the meaning of "he built it" is: he ordered its building. But since this building could only happen by his order, it is attributed to him. So God takes the souls; their taking happens only by His command, so the taking is attributed to Him.

As for His saying ﴿تَوَفَّتْهُ رُسُلُنَا﴾ [Al-An'am 61] and His saying ﴿قُلْ يَتَوَفَّاكُمْ مَلَكُ الْمَوْتِ﴾ [As-Sajdah 11], either it is said that ﴿مَلَكُ الْمَوْتِ﴾ here is a singular in construct, so it is general, encompassing the angels. This has a basis in the Arabic language, but it is not accurate in terms of reality. The reality is that the angel of death has assistants both before the seizing of the soul and after it. Before the seizing, they drive the soul out of the body until it reaches the throat, and then he seizes it. After that, when he has seized it, there are angels of mercy waiting for this soul with a shroud from Paradise, and they do not leave it in his hand for an instant until they take it and put it in that shroud. If the person is the opposite, may God save us, there are angels of punishment with them, with a shroud of fire, and they do not leave it in his hand for an instant. So here the intended meaning is to combine both.

As for the attribution of taking to the messengers (the angels), in the plural, because they are the assistants of the angel of death, they have a kind of participation in this action. The angel of death is the one who seizes it when it reaches the throat.

With this combination the difficulty disappears. We have explained many times that the Qur'an and the Sunnah contain no contradiction: ﴿وَلَوْ كَانَ مِنْ عِنْدِ غَيْرِ اللَّهِ لَوَجَدُوا فِيهِ اخْتِلَافًا كَثِيرًا﴾ "Had it been from other than God, they would have found in it much contradiction" [An-Nisa' 82]. If you see a contradiction in either of them, know that it is due to a fault in your understanding or your lack of knowledge. So reflect and learn until the matter becomes clear to you.

* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, but the one who takes it directly from the throat is the angel of death. Then those angels who have stretched out their hands, if they are the ones waiting to seize it, they wait to seize it and take it from him. If they are the others who bring it out until it reaches the throat, then likewise, there is no difficulty.

﴿قُلْ يَتَوَفَّاكُمْ مَلَكُ الْمَوْتِ الَّذِي وُكِّلَ بِكُمْ ثُمَّ إِلَى رَبِّكُمْ تُرْجَعُونَ﴾ "Say: The angel of death who has been entrusted with you will take you; then to your Lord you will be returned" [As-Sajdah 11]. The author says: (﴿الَّذِي وُكِّلَ بِكُمْ﴾ means: to seize your souls.) That is: he has not been entrusted with us in everything, but only with seizing souls. However, there are angels entrusted with us for recording our deeds and also for protecting us. Likewise there are angels entrusted with our deeds who roam the earth and look for gatherings of remembrance, and sit in them.

(﴿ثُمَّ إِلَى رَبِّكُمْ تُرْجَعُونَ﴾ [As-Sajdah 11], alive, so He will recompense you for your deeds.) That is, after death a person returns to his Lord and is recompensed for his deeds: if good, then good, and if evil, then evil.

Then He, Most High, said: (﴿وَلَوْ تَرَى إِذِ الْمُجْرِمُونَ﴾ "If only you could see when the criminals," i.e. the disbelievers, ﴿نَاكِسُو رُءُوسِهِمْ عِنْدَ رَبِّهِمْ﴾ "are bowing their heads before their Lord," i.e. lowering them in shame, saying: ﴿رَبَّنَا أَبْصَرْنَا﴾ "Our Lord, we have seen," i.e. we no longer deny the resurrection, ﴿وَسَمِعْنَا﴾ "and we have heard," from You, the confirmation of the messengers in what we denied them, ﴿فَارْجِعْنَا﴾ "so send us back" to the world, ﴿نَعْمَلْ صَالِحًا﴾ "that we may do righteousness" in it, ﴿إِنَّا مُوقِنُونَ﴾ "indeed we are certain" now [As-Sajdah 12].)

﴿وَلَوْ تَرَى إِذِ الْمُجْرِمُونَ﴾: the address in ﴿وَلَوْ تَرَى﴾ is either to the Messenger ﷺ, or to everyone to whom the address is directed. This second meaning is more general, and adopting it is preferable because of its generality, unless some impediment prevents it. For this reason, the addresses in the singular found throughout the Qur'an should preferably be understood in a general sense, meaning everyone to whom the address is directed, unless something prevents that, in which case it is specific to the Messenger ﷺ.

His saying ﴿لَوْ تَرَى﴾: "law" here is conditional. The conditional "law" requires an answer, i.e. a condition and an answer to the condition. The condition is "you see," and the answer is omitted. Its estimated meaning: you would see a dreadful matter.

His saying ﴿لَوْ تَرَى إِذِ الْمُجْرِمُونَ نَاكِسُو رُءُوسِهِمْ﴾ [As-Sajdah 12]: "idh" here is an adverb of time, meaning: if you could see that time when the criminals are in this state, you would see a dreadful matter. ﴿إِذِ الْمُجْرِمُونَ﴾ is the subject, and ﴿نَاكِسُو﴾ is the predicate. Where is the nun in ﴿نَاكِسُو﴾? It was dropped because of the annexation (*idafah*). ﴿نَاكِسُو رُءُوسِهِمْ﴾ means: lowering them, i.e. bowing them down, may God save us.

﴿عِنْدَ رَبِّهِمْ﴾ means: before God, Mighty and Majestic, and they stand before Him on the Day of Resurrection. But the author says they lower them out of shame, and there is something in the soul about this explanation. The apparent meaning, however, is that they lower them in humiliation and submission to God's authority, as evidenced by His saying ﴿رَبَّنَا أَبْصَرْنَا﴾ [As-Sajdah 12]. As for shame, shame is praiseworthy, but their lowering their heads in humiliation is the reality.

﴿نَاكِسُو رُءُوسِهِمْ عِنْدَ رَبِّهِمْ﴾ in humiliation, as God, Most High, said: ﴿وَتَرَاهُمْ يُعْرَضُونَ عَلَيْهَا خَاشِعِينَ مِنَ الذُّلِّ يَنْظُرُونَ مِنْ طَرْفٍ خَفِيٍّ﴾ "And you will see them exposed to it, humbled by humiliation, looking with a sidelong glance" [Ash-Shura 45].

﴿عِنْدَ رَبِّهِمْ﴾ they say: ﴿رَبَّنَا أَبْصَرْنَا﴾. The clause ﴿رَبَّنَا أَبْصَرْنَا﴾ is a quotation of an omitted saying, its estimated form being: they say, "Our Lord, we have seen." That is: "O our Lord." They call upon God by the name of Lordship, because most supplicatory sentences begin with "Rabb," since *rabb* means the owner who disposes of things.

﴿رَبَّنَا أَبْصَرْنَا﴾: the author says: (we no longer deny the resurrection). This is what the author said, and accordingly the object of ﴿أَبْصَرْنَا﴾ is omitted, the estimate being: we no longer deny the resurrection. It may also mean that ﴿أَبْصَرْنَا﴾ here means: our sight and insight have been opened, so it is more general than what the author estimated. That is: we have now become people of sight and insight. This meaning is more general and more eloquent.

Likewise ﴿وَسَمِعْنَا﴾. The author says: (﴿وَسَمِعْنَا﴾ from You, the confirmation of the messengers in what we denied them), because God, Most High, says: ﴿هَذَا مَا وَعَدَ الرَّحْمَنُ وَصَدَقَ الْمُرْسَلُونَ﴾ "This is what the Most Merciful promised, and the messengers told the truth" [Ya-Sin 52]. But also, what the author said has a better aspect than what he said: the meaning of "we heard" is that we have now become people of hearing. For this reason they say: ﴿لَوْ كُنَّا نَسْمَعُ أَوْ نَعْقِلُ مَا كُنَّا فِي أَصْحَابِ السَّعِيرِ﴾ "Had we been listening or reasoning, we would not have been among the companions of the Blaze" [Al-Mulk 10], in the world. But on the Day of Resurrection they say: yes, now we have become people of sight and people of hearing.

﴿فَارْجِعْنَا نَعْمَلْ﴾ [As-Sajdah 12]: "send us back" to the world. It is a verb of request, i.e. supplication, not a verb of command, because a created being does not direct a command to the Creator.

His saying ﴿نَعْمَلْ﴾ is the answer to the request. It is in the jussive mood because of the answer to a request. Meaning: if You send us back, we will do righteousness.

His saying ﴿نَعْمَلْ صَالِحًا﴾ means: a righteous deed. A righteous deed has been mentioned many times as that which combines two conditions: sincerity to God, glorified and exalted, and following the Messenger ﷺ. This is the righteous deed.

﴿نَعْمَلْ صَالِحًا﴾. He says: (in it, ﴿إِنَّا مُوقِنُونَ﴾ "indeed we are certain" now). Then it is known that this will not benefit them, and they will not be returned. When they witness the punishment, faith does not benefit them. Everyone who witnesses punishment, faith does not benefit him: ﴿فَلَمَّا رَأَوْا بَأْسَنَا قَالُوا آمَنَّا بِاللَّهِ وَحْدَهُ وَكَفَرْنَا بِمَا كُنَّا بِهِ مُشْرِكِينَ﴾ "But when they saw Our punishment they said: We believe in God alone, and we disbelieve in what we used to associate with Him" [Ghafir 84]. God, Most High, said: ﴿فَلَمْ يَكُ يَنْفَعُهُمْ إِيمَانُهُمْ لَمَّا رَأَوْا بَأْسَنَا سُنَّةَ اللَّهِ الَّتِي قَدْ خَلَتْ فِي عِبَادِهِ وَخَسِرَ هُنَالِكَ الْكَافِرُونَ﴾ "Their faith did not benefit them when they saw Our punishment; this is God's way which has already passed among His servants, and there the disbelievers lost" [Ghafir 85]. No one's faith benefited him after seeing the punishment except one town: the people of Yunus, when they believed, God removed the punishment from them. For this reason God, Most High, said: ﴿وَلَيْسَتِ التَّوْبَةُ لِلَّذِينَ يَعْمَلُونَ السَّيِّئَاتِ حَتَّى إِذَا حَضَرَ أَحَدَهُمُ الْمَوْتُ قَالَ إِنِّي تُبْتُ الْآنَ﴾ "Repentance is not for those who do evil deeds until, when death approaches one of them, he says: Now I have repented" [An-Nisa' 18]. Does he have repentance now? It is seen: he has witnessed the punishment, so it does not benefit him. For this reason a person must hasten to use his life before his term comes upon him, and then he cannot escape.

﴿فَارْجِعْنَا نَعْمَلْ صَالِحًا إِنَّا مُوقِنُونَ﴾ [As-Sajdah 12]. They used the nominal sentence, which indicates permanence and continuity: ﴿إِنَّا مُوقِنُونَ﴾ "indeed we are certain." When? Now. But it does not benefit. What is your opinion: if they were returned, what would the matter be?

* Student: They would return to what they were forbidden.
* Shaykh: They would return to what they were forbidden: ﴿وَلَوْ تَرَى إِذْ وُقِفُوا عَلَى النَّارِ فَقَالُوا يَا لَيْتَنَا نُرَدُّ وَلَا نُكَذِّبَ بِآيَاتِ رَبِّنَا وَنَكُونَ مِنَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ (27) بَلْ بَدَا لَهُمْ مَا كَانُوا يُخْفُونَ مِنْ قَبْلُ وَلَوْ رُدُّوا لَعَادُوا لِمَا نُهُوا عَنْهُ﴾ "If only you could see when they are made to stand over the Fire and say: 'Would that we were returned, and we would not deny the signs of our Lord, and we would be among the believers.' (27) Rather, there has appeared to them what they used to conceal before. And if they were returned, they would certainly return to what they were forbidden." This is the report of God, Mighty and Majestic, which He does not break. ﴿وَإِنَّهُمْ لَكَاذِبُونَ﴾ "And indeed they are liars" [Al-An'am 27–28].

* Student: Shaykh, but there is a condition here (...) that if they were returned, they would return.
* Shaykh: I do not know. As long as God says this, whatever comes after the words of God is not words. The statement is clear: ﴿وَلَوْ تَرَى إِذْ وُقِفُوا عَلَى النَّارِ ... وَلَوْ رُدُّوا لَعَادُوا لِمَا نُهُوا عَنْهُ﴾.

* Student: And the sinners (*fussaq*)?
* Shaykh: The sinners, no. What is meant is the disbelievers. The sinners do not remain in the Fire forever; they are punished according to their deeds, and then they enter Paradise. The sinners cross the Bridge (*sirat*); they are not taken to the Fire. They cross the Bridge, and then they fall into the Fire according to their deeds.

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: (...) like the Jews and Christians, for example, for whom it does not benefit, since they disbelieved.

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes indeed. Among the present-day atheists, some hold that this worldly life is their only life: they die and live, and that is all, and they have no book or anything. Either he says this out of conviction, or he says it out of imitation and obstinacy.

God, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿وَلَوْ شِئْنَا﴾ "And had We willed" [As-Sajdah 13]. The author says: (The answer to "law" is: you would have seen a dreadful matter), meaning the answer is omitted.

If someone asks: what is the wisdom in omitting the answer? Why is it not mentioned, so that there is no disagreement? And what is the wisdom in the vagueness in His saying: ﴿فَغَشِيَهُمْ مِنَ الْيَمِّ مَا غَشِيَهُمْ﴾ "So the sea covered them, that which covered them" [Ta-Ha 78]? And why is it not mentioned, since it would be clearer?

The answer: in a context of awe-inspiring magnitude (*tahwil*, emphasizing the terrifying gravity of a matter), it is appropriate to leave things vague, so that the mind goes in every direction in magnifying the matter and its dread. For if a thing is named, it may seem less frightening. Suppose someone said to you: "By God, there is a great beast in it that devours people, and does this and that and that," and you were made to dread it, though you have not seen it. You would feel terror. But perhaps when you actually see it, the matter becomes less daunting to you. Likewise, when God leaves such great matters unspecified, they are greater, strike the soul more forcefully, and are more severe and immense. For this reason the response is omitted here, and the enveloping thing is left unspecified in His saying: ﴿Then there covered them of the sea that which covered them﴾. Likewise, *al-Haqqah* and *al-Qari'ah* are left unspecified in such verses as: ﴿The Inevitable Reality. What is the Inevitable Reality? And what will make you know what the Inevitable Reality is?﴾ and ﴿The Striking Calamity. What is the Striking Calamity?﴾ and what is similar to these. All of this is by way of magnification and awe-inspiring emphasis.

He says: ﴿And had We willed, We would have given every soul its guidance﴾ [al-Sajdah 13]. "O Allah, guide us among those whom You have guided." ﴿And had We willed, We would have given every soul its guidance﴾ (so that it would be guided to faith and obedience by its own choice).

As for ﴿had We willed﴾: the pronoun refers to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and He used the plural pronoun as a mark of magnificence. If the Christian says, "The gods are three," and Allah says, ﴿And had We willed﴾ here, [the Christian argues that this is] plural. Produce for us a proof that removes this expression from its meaning; otherwise the truth is with us, and you, O monotheists, are in error. Otherwise, would Allah have said: "And had I willed"?

The answer: this is a case of deception and confusion. Return to His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And your God is One God; there is no deity except Him, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful﴾ [al-Baqarah 163]. How many does that make? One. So ﴿had We willed﴾ is for magnification. ﴿And had We willed﴾ is by way of magnification, and Allah, the Exalted, is great in His attributes. Each of His attributes entails a greatness different from what the other attribute entails, and by the combination of these attributes there is a greater and more exalted majesty.

﴿And had We willed﴾ [al-Sajdah 13]: this is the first answer. ﴿Lā'atayna﴾ means "We would have given." For this reason it takes two objects: the first object is ﴿every soul﴾, and the second is ﴿its guidance﴾. *Al-hudā* means guidance in the sense of indication and success (*tawfiq*). For this reason he said: (so that it would be guided to faith and obedience).

If Allah, the Exalted, had willed, He would have done it, as He said in another verse: ﴿And if your Lord had willed, He would have made mankind one community, but they will continue to differ, except those upon whom your Lord has mercy; and for that He created them﴾ [Hud 118-119]. So if Allah willed, He would have made mankind one community upon faith, monotheism, and steadfastness. But the wisdom of Allah refuses that, for many reasons. Among them: He, the Majestic and Exalted, said to Hell: ﴿I will surely fill Hell with jinn and mankind, all together﴾ [al-Sajdah 13]. ﴿I will surely fill﴾ is an oath and a binding commitment from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, to Hell that He will fill it. ﴿I will surely fill Hell with jinn...﴾

If mankind were one community upon monotheism, would this have come true or not? It would not have come true. Therefore it must come true.

Second: If mankind were one community upon monotheism, would the believer be distinguished from the disbeliever? They would all be one. There would be no trial or test. And if mankind were one community upon monotheism, the enjoining of good and forbidding of evil would be closed off. Why? Because there would be no evil to require forbidding it. And if mankind were one community upon monotheism, would jihad be nullified or not? Whom would we fight? There would be no one.

The point is that there are many wisdoms in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, making people into two categories. For this reason He said here: ﴿But the word from Me has come into effect﴾ [al-Sajdah 13]. ﴿Haqqa﴾ means "became obligatory and established," ﴿al-qawlu﴾ is the subject, and ﴿minnī﴾ is attached to an implied element as a circumstantial qualifier of the word: ﴿But the word has come into effect﴾, issuing ﴿from Me﴾. What is this word? ﴿I will surely fill Hell with jinn and mankind, all together﴾ [al-Sajdah 13]. Here the verb is emphasized with the *nūn* and the *lām* and the implied oath. Is this emphasis grammatically obligatory or not? It is obligatory, because it is an affirmative future oath with no separation between it and its *lām*.

As for His saying ﴿la'amla'anna Jahannam﴾ (I will surely fill Hell): *Jahannam* is one of the names of the Fire. It has been said that it is Arabic, with the *nūn* being extra, and that it is derived from *al-jahm* or *al-tajahhum*, which means darkness. It has also been said that it is an arabized loanword (*mu'arrab*), not Arabic, but arabized. Under all the opinions, what is meant by it is the Fire. We ask Allah for well-being.

﴿I will surely fill Hell with the jinn and mankind﴾ [al-Sajdah 13]: *al-jinnah* means the jinn, and ﴿mankind﴾ means the children of Adam. ﴿All together﴾ means it will be filled with these and those. Which of them is more numerous?

* Students: Allah knows best.
* The Shaykh: Allah knows best. But the apparent division is that they are equal: ﴿from the jinn and mankind﴾.

Do the jinn enter the Fire? It has been understood now from this verse and from another verse that they enter it, as He said: ﴿He will say, "Enter into the Fire among nations that had passed away before you of jinn and men"﴾ [al-A'raf 38]. They enter the Fire. There is a consensus of the Muslims that the disbelieving jinn enter the Fire. Do the believing jinn enter Paradise or not?

The scholars differed about this. The correct view is that they enter Paradise. Allah said: ﴿O assembly of jinn and mankind, did there not come to you messengers from among you, relating to you My verses?...﴾ Then whoever is righteous and reforms, from where? From the jinn and mankind: ﴿Then whoever fears Allah and reforms, there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve. But those who denied Our verses and were arrogant toward them, those are the companions of the Fire, wherein they will abide forever﴾ [al-A'raf 35-36].

He said: ﴿But for he who fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾ [al-Rahman 46], then ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ [al-Rahman 47], addressing whom? The jinn and mankind. This is also evidence that they enter Paradise.

Likewise His saying: ﴿Before them neither man nor jinn has touched them﴾ [al-Rahman 56] indicates that they enter Paradise. This is the view of the majority of the scholars.

Some of them said that they do not enter Paradise, because those who turned back to their people as warners said: ﴿O our people, indeed we have heard a Book revealed after Moses, confirming what was before it, guiding to the truth and to a straight path. O our people, respond to the caller of Allah and believe in him; He will forgive you of your sins and protect you from a painful punishment﴾ [al-Ahqaf 30-31]. They did not say, "He will admit you into Paradise." This indicates that the believer among them is only protected from the painful punishment.

It is said: this is an argument using one text while abandoning other texts. This is not how a person behaves who reconciles the evidences. Furthermore, the station of these people is a station of warning and fear: ﴿They turned back to their people as warners﴾ [al-Ahqaf 29], not as bringers of good tidings (...).

Isn't that so? I think if a cow were made to compete in a contest for a position, would it compete? No, of course not, because that is not its concern. But if fodder were placed in a corner of the house, would it race toward it? Yes, it would race toward it, because Allah guided every creature to what suits it.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the refutation of the theory (...), which is the theory of Darwin, who says that creation arose through evolution and that the origin of man is an ape, which over the length of time became a human. On his principle we do not know what man will become over the length of time. There is no doubt that this theory is false and is disbelief in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. We derive this from His saying: ﴿And He began the creation of man from clay﴾ [al-Sajdah 7]. Nothing is more explicit than this verse: ﴿And He began the creation of man from clay﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the perfection of His power, may He be blessed and exalted, in that He created this wondrous man, in his creation, understanding, management, and intelligence, from this inert thing, which is clay.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of Allah's voluntary acts, which are connected to His will. From where is this derived? From His saying: ﴿And He began﴾, for beginning is from non-existence.

* Among its benefits: that man is originated, having not existed before, from His saying: ﴿And He began﴾.

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Then He made his descendants from an extract of a liquid, despised﴾ [al-Sajdah 8].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that this man who was created from clay has offspring. Offspring was made for him so that this kind of creature would continue, from His saying: ﴿Then He made his descendants﴾.

* Among its benefits: that man is created from semen, from His saying: ﴿his descendants from an extract﴾ [al-Sajdah 8]. *Al-sulālah* is the essence, and *al-mā' al-mahīn* (the despised fluid) is semen. On this basis, he is created from the semen of the man, not the semen of the woman, since the verse says *al-mā' al-mahīn* (the despised fluid).

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the wisdom of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in this fluid, in that He made it of this weakness and this kind, in order to preserve the sperm. For if it were as liquid as water, it would not retain these cells. And if it were thicker than this, it would harm these cells, perhaps killing them. But Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, placed it in this state (...).

Then He said: ﴿Then He proportioned him and breathed into him of His spirit﴾ (to the end of the verse) [al-Sajdah 9].

* It is derived from these noble verses: that Allah, the Exalted, perfected the creation of man, from His saying: ﴿Then He proportioned him﴾. This is supported by His saying: ﴿We have certainly created man in the best of stature﴾ [al-Tin 4], and His saying: ﴿He shaped you and perfected your forms﴾ [Ghafir 64].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that man is a body that is not a human except by the spirit, from His saying: ﴿And breathed into him of His spirit﴾ [al-Sajdah 9].

* Among them (though it is not a strong view): that the spirit is a body, since it is breathed into this perishing body. And indeed the spirit is a body, but a subtle body that is not seen. Yet the angels take it, place it in the funerary spices, and ascend with it to the heaven. But we do not see it when the soul of the dead departs. Do we see anything in him? No, we see nothing.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the demonstration of Allah's blessing upon man in giving him hearing, sight, and hearts, by which he perceives the intelligible. Perceiving the intelligible by what? By hearing and sight. And understanding it? By the heart and its awareness.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that man is little in thanks, from His saying: ﴿Little are you grateful﴾ [al-Sajdah 9]. Just as the grateful are few, and those who fulfill gratitude in the required manner are few. Allah said: ﴿And few of My servants are grateful﴾ [Saba' 13].

* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: The grateful are few because, in terms of individuals and persons, one in ten is grateful, and this is few. The gratitude of the single individual is also little, and the grateful person's gratitude is also little. So His saying ﴿Little are you grateful﴾ [al-Sajdah 9] is in terms of the gratitude of the grateful, while His saying ﴿And few of My servants are grateful﴾ [Saba' 13] is in terms of the number of grateful individuals.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the censure of one who does not give thanks, from His saying: ﴿Little are you grateful﴾ [al-Sajdah 9].

* Among its benefits: that a person should make his gratitude proportionate to the blessing. In the case of hearing, he uses his hearing for what brings him closer to Allah, and restrains it from what Allah has forbidden. Likewise with sight. As for the heart, it is obligatory upon it to turn away from everything Allah has forbidden, and to turn toward everything Allah has commanded.

Then the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And they say, "When we are lost in the earth, will we indeed be in a new creation?"﴾ [al-Sajdah 10].

* Derived from this noble verse: the rebuke of these deniers, as will come at its end: ﴿Rather, they are disbelievers in the meeting with their Lord﴾ [al-Sajdah 10].

* Among its benefits: that these deniers were doubtful about the power of Allah, from their saying: ﴿When we are lost﴾ and ﴿will we indeed be﴾.
It is possible that this was obstinacy on their part, and that they knew the power of Allah but were stubborn. This is supported by His saying: ﴿Rather, they are disbelievers in the meeting with their Lord﴾, meaning the matter is clear, but these are disbelievers.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the perfection of Allah's power, the Mighty and Majestic, in restoring the dead after they had vanished into the earth and dissolved in it, Allah bringing them forth as a new creation.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the refutation of the saying of one who says that resurrection is bringing into existence from non-existence. For there are those who say that this creation is totally annihilated and then brought into being anew. This view is false, because if it were so, reward would be for one who did not act, and punishment for one who did not act. If we say he is annihilated completely and then a new creation arises and is held to account, this new one is not the original, so he would be punished for what he did not do and rewarded for what he did not do. Allah, the Exalted, has made clear that the person himself is what is restored. He is not annihilated and then created anew, but he is restored: ﴿As We began the first creation, We will repeat it﴾ [al-Anbiya' 104]. He did not say, "We will create another." The evidence is His saying: ﴿When we are lost in the earth, will we indeed be in a new creation?﴾ [al-Sajdah 10]. ("When we are lost": they say, "How, after we are hidden in the earth and become dust, will we be resurrected?") This shows that resurrection is the restoration of what previously existed, not the beginning of a new creation.

* Among the benefits of the verse: that these deniers of resurrection have no proof except mere disbelief, from His saying: ﴿Rather, they are disbelievers in the meeting with their Lord﴾ [al-Sajdah 10].

* Among its benefits: the affirmation of meeting Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, on the Day of Resurrection, from His saying: ﴿meeting﴾. Similar to it is His saying: ﴿O mankind, indeed you are laboring toward your Lord with labor, and you will meet Him﴾ [al-Inshiqaq 6].

He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Say, "The angel of death who has been charged with you will take your souls"﴾ (to the end) [al-Sajdah 11].

* It is derived from this noble verse: that the one who takes charge of seizing souls is the Angel of Death, from His saying: ﴿Say, "The Angel of Death will take you"﴾.

* Among its benefits: the affirmation of the angels, from His saying: ﴿the Angel of Death﴾.
